records.source: Jones, Graham M. 2021. “Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat.” In Experimenting with Ethnography: A Companion to Analysis, edited by Andrea Ballestero and Brit Ross Winthereik, 151–162. Durham, NC: Duke University Press, pp. 151, 160–161.
records.text:
> We gather data according to preestablished categories of theoretical and comparative concern, and we also require that the way our subjects categorize salient features of their experience shape what we record.
>
> — Graham M. Jones, "Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat," p. 151

> In making a filing system you have probably already used native categories; now make sure you also include native categorization practices—for instance, recurrent analogies—as file headings.
>
> — Graham M. Jones, "Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat," p. 161

In anthropology, “native” means belonging to the people studied, as opposed to the outside analyst. Jones separates native categories (the kinds into which people sort things) from native categorization practices (how they sort: labels, concepts, metaphors, analogies), and he asks researchers to treat both as headings in their files.

records.title: Analogy as categorization
records.description: To draw an analogy is to put two things in one category while marking their differences, and Jones diagrams this as a base mapped onto a target to produce a concept.
records.source: Jones, Graham M. 2021. “Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat.” In Experimenting with Ethnography: A Companion to Analysis, edited by Andrea Ballestero and Brit Ross Winthereik, 151–162. Durham, NC: Duke University Press, pp. 158–159.
records.text:
> Positing a cross-cultural analogy is also a mode of categorization—in the case I was considering, one that framed French illusionism and ‘Isawa rituals as somehow examples of the same thing (“magic”) but with crucial differences.
>
> — Graham M. Jones, "Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat," p. 158

> culture consists in the way people draw analogies between different domains of their worlds.
>
> — Marilyn Strathern, Reproducing the Future (1992), quoted in Jones, Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat, p. 159

Following the psychologist Dedre Gentner, Jones describes analogy as mapping patterns from a familiar base domain onto an unfamiliar target domain, which yields an abstract concept; he draws it as a triangle with the base at lower left, the target at lower right, and the concept at the top. French writers mapped Western stage magic onto ‘Isawa ritual and produced the concept of “primitive magic,” an analogy Jones calls “inaccurate, tendentious, and racist” but culturally productive for claims of French superiority (p. 158).

records.title: Meta-analogy
records.description: An analogy between two groups' analogies, which Jones used to show how anthropologists and stage magicians together built the idea of a disenchanted modern West.
records.source: Jones, Graham M. 2021. “Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat.” In Experimenting with Ethnography: A Companion to Analysis, edited by Andrea Ballestero and Brit Ross Winthereik, 151–162. Durham, NC: Duke University Press, pp. 159–160.
records.text:
> I called my comparison between analogy-making practices in anthropology and analogy-making practices in magic a “meta-analogy.”
>
> — Graham M. Jones, "Categorize, Recategorize, Repeat," pp. 159–160

Both anthropologists and modern magicians compared “modern” and “primitive” magic. Comparing those two sets of comparisons, and diagramming them with the same base-target-concept triangle, showed Jones how experts in both fields reinforced a shared idea of disenchantment as distinctive of Western modernity, the argument of his book Magic's Reason. He notes that the method suits few projects, but it points to something general: the ways people categorize can themselves be compared and categorized.

records.title: The magic circle
records.description: A game takes place inside a boundary, in space or in agreement, where its own rules hold and ordinary life is set aside.
records.source: Johan Huizinga, Homo Ludens: A Study of the Play-Element in Culture (Dutch original 1938; English edition Roy Publishers, 1950; Beacon Press paperback, 1955), p. 10; Katie Salen and Eric Zimmerman, Rules of Play: Game Design Fundamentals (MIT Press, 2004 [2003]), pp. 95–96, as quoted in Jesper Juul, "The Magic Circle and the Puzzle Piece," in Stephan Günzel, Michael Liebe and Dieter Mersch, eds., Conference Proceedings of the Philosophy of Computer Games 2008 (Potsdam: University Press, 2008), pp. 56–67, p. 57; Eric Zimmerman, "Jerked Around by the Magic Circle: Clearing the Air Ten Years Later," Gamasutra, 2012.
records.text:
> The arena, the card-table, the magic circle, the temple, the stage, the screen, the tennis court, the court of justice, etc., are all in form and function play-grounds, i.e. forbidden spots, isolated, hedged round, hallowed, within which special rules obtain. All are temporary worlds within the ordinary world, dedicated to the performance of an act apart.
>
> — Johan Huizinga, *Homo Ludens*, p. 10

> In a very basic sense, the magic circle of a game is where the game takes place. To play a game means entering into a magic circle, or perhaps creating one as a game begins.
>
> — Katie Salen and Eric Zimmerman, Rules of Play (2004), pp. 95–96, as quoted in Jesper Juul, "The Magic Circle and the Puzzle Piece" (2008), p. 57

> The magic circle is the idea that a boundary exists between a game and the world outside the game.
>
> — Eric Zimmerman, "Jerked Around by the Magic Circle: Clearing the Air Ten Years Later" (2012), https://www.ericzimmerman.com/assets/pdfs/MCJ_Zimmerman.pdf

Huizinga used "magic circle" once in a list of set-apart places, the card table, the stage and the court of justice among them, where special rules hold for a while. Game designers Frank Lantz and Eric Zimmerman took up the phrase in their teaching around 1999, and Salen and Zimmerman's Rules of Play made it the standard name for the boundary around a game. Zimmerman later wrote that neither Huizinga nor Rules of Play claimed that games are completely separate from the rest of life. The circle is better understood as an agreement among players than as a wall.

See also: [huizinga](/cards/huizinga) · [salen zimmerman](/cards/salen-zimmerman)

records.title: Play (Huizinga's definition)
records.description: Play is a free activity, set apart from ordinary life in time and place, that follows fixed rules and absorbs the player completely.
records.source: Johan Huizinga, Homo Ludens: A Study of the Play-Element in Culture (Dutch original 1938; English edition Roy Publishers, 1950; Beacon Press paperback, 1955), pp. 8, 13.
records.text:
> Here, then, we have the first main characteristic of play: that it is free, is in fact freedom.
>
> — Johan Huizinga, *Homo Ludens*, p. 8

> Summing up the formal characteristics of play we might call it a free activity standing quite consciously outside "ordinary" life as being "not serious", but at the same time absorbing the player intensely and utterly. It is an activity connected with no material interest, and no profit can be gained by it. It proceeds within its own proper boundaries of time and space according to fixed rules and in an orderly manner.
>
> — Johan Huizinga, *Homo Ludens*, p. 13

Huizinga, a Dutch historian, lists the features of play: it is voluntary, it steps outside ordinary life, it is limited in time and place, it has fixed rules that create order, and it brings no profit. Play can feel "not serious" and still absorb people completely. His larger claim is that play is older than culture and runs through serious institutions such as law, war and ritual.

See also: [huizinga](/cards/huizinga)

records.title: Agôn, alea, mimicry, ilinx
records.description: Caillois sorts games into four kinds: competition (agôn), chance (alea), make-believe (mimicry) and vertigo (ilinx).
records.source: Roger Caillois, Man, Play and Games, trans. Meyer Barash (Free Press, 1961; University of Illinois Press, 2001; French original Les jeux et les hommes, 1958), as quoted in Thomas S. Henricks, "Caillois's Man, Play, and Games: An Appreciation and Evaluation," American Journal of Play 3, no. 2 (Fall 2010), pp. 167–169.
records.text:
> In the former, the player “tries to vanquish a rival operating under the same conditions as himself”: in the latter, the player “merely awaits the outcome”
>
> — Thomas S. Henricks, quoting Roger Caillois on agôn and alea, "Caillois's Man, Play, and Games: An Appreciation and Evaluation", p. 167

> There, the player tries to “escape himself and become another.”
>
> — Thomas S. Henricks, quoting Roger Caillois on mimicry, "Caillois's Man, Play, and Games: An Appreciation and Evaluation", p. 168

> The final type of play is ilinx, the pursuit of vertigo, which consists “of an attempt to momentarily destroy the stability of perception and inflict a kind of voluptuous panic upon an otherwise lucid mind”
>
> — Thomas S. Henricks, quoting Roger Caillois, "Caillois's Man, Play, and Games: An Appreciation and Evaluation", p. 169

Roger Caillois, writing in French in 1958 (English 1961), built on Huizinga by sorting games by the attitude they ask of players. In agôn players compete on equal terms and skill decides; in alea they give themselves up to chance; in mimicry they pretend to be someone else; in ilinx they seek dizziness and disorder. He also placed every game on a scale from paidia, free improvised play ("diversion, turbulence, free improvisation, and carefree gaiety"), to ludus, play bound by "arbitrary, imperative, and purposively tedious conventions" (both quoted in Henricks, p. 167). Many games, and many real systems such as markets, mix agôn and alea.

See also: [caillois](/cards/caillois) · [huizinga](/cards/huizinga)

records.title: MDA: mechanics, dynamics, aesthetics
records.description: A game can be read in three linked layers: the rules (mechanics), the behaviour that comes out of them in play (dynamics), and what players feel (aesthetics).
records.source: Robin Hunicke, Marc LeBlanc and Robert Zubek, "MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research," AAAI Workshop Papers 2004 (WS-04-04), p. 2, https://cdn.aaai.org/Workshops/2004/WS-04-04/WS04-04-001.pdf
records.text:
> Mechanics describes the particular components of the game, at the level of data representation and algorithms.
>
> — Robin Hunicke, Marc LeBlanc and Robert Zubek, "MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research", p. 2

> Dynamics describes the run-time behavior of the mechanics acting on player inputs and each others’ outputs over time.
>
> — Robin Hunicke, Marc LeBlanc and Robert Zubek, "MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research", p. 2

> Aesthetics describes the desirable emotional responses evoked in the player, when she interacts with the game system.
>
> — Robin Hunicke, Marc LeBlanc and Robert Zubek, "MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research", p. 2

> From the designer’s perspective, the mechanics give rise to dynamic system behavior, which in turn leads to particular aesthetic experiences.
>
> — Robin Hunicke, Marc LeBlanc and Robert Zubek, "MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research", p. 2

MDA came out of a game design workshop taught at the Game Developers Conference from 2001 to 2004. Designers write mechanics, the rules and data; dynamics are what those rules do once players act on them; aesthetics are the feelings that result, such as challenge, discovery or fellowship. A designer works from mechanics outward, while a player meets the game from aesthetics inward, so a small change in a rule can change how the whole game feels. The authors say the content of a game is its behaviour, not the pictures and sounds on the screen.

See also: [schell](/cards/schell)

records.title: Game mechanics
records.description: A game mechanic is an action a player can take that changes the state of the game.
records.source: Miguel Sicart, "Defining Game Mechanics," Game Studies 8, no. 2 (2008), http://gamestudies.org/0802/articles/sicart
records.text:
> game mechanics are methods invoked by agents, designed for interaction with the game state
>
> — Miguel Sicart, "Defining Game Mechanics", Game Studies 8, no. 2 (2008)

Sicart defines mechanics as the verbs of a game: jump, build, trade, inspect, attack. The rules set what is possible, and the mechanics are what an agent, a player or a computer-controlled character, actually does to change the game's state. Many critics read a game's values from its mechanics: what a game lets you do, and what it never lets you do, shows what kind of world it describes.

See also: [sicart](/cards/sicart) · [the checkpoint](/mechanics/the-checkpoint) · [labor allocation](/mechanics/labor-allocation)

records.title: Emergence and progression
records.description: Games challenge players in two basic ways: a few rules that combine into endless variety (emergence), or a set series of challenges met one after another (progression).
records.source: Jesper Juul, "The Open and the Closed: Games of Emergence and Games of Progression," in Frans Mäyrä, ed., Computer Games and Digital Cultures Conference Proceedings (Tampere University Press, 2002), pp. 323–329, https://www.jesperjuul.net/text/openandtheclosed.html; see also Jesper Juul, Half-Real: Video Games between Real Rules and Fictional Worlds (MIT Press, 2005).
records.text:
> most computer games are the combination of two different ways of presenting the player with a challenge, one which I will term emergence (simple rules combining, leading to variation) and one of progression (serially introduced challenges).
>
> — Jesper Juul, "The Open and the Closed: Games of Emergence and Games of Progression", https://www.jesperjuul.net/text/openandtheclosed.html

> In progression games, the player has to perform a predefined set of actions in order to complete the game.
>
> — Jesper Juul, "The Open and the Closed: Games of Emergence and Games of Progression", https://www.jesperjuul.net/text/openandtheclosed.html

Chess, card games and strategy games are games of emergence: a small set of rules produces situations the designer never wrote down, and players invent strategies for them. Adventure games are games of progression: the designer sets the sequence, which suits storytelling, and a walkthrough can list every step. Juul says emergence is the older structure and progression entered with computer adventure games; most games mix the two. He develops the distinction further in Half-Real (2005).

See also: [juul](/cards/juul) · [tech tree and unlocks](/mechanics/tech-tree-and-unlocks) · [cascade failure](/mechanics/cascade-failure) · [spread](/mechanics/spread)

records.title: The lusory attitude
records.description: To play a game is to accept rules that forbid the easy way, just so that the game can happen.
records.source: Bernard Suits, "The Elements of Sport" (1973), in William J. Morgan, ed., Ethics in Sport (Human Kinetics, 2007), pp. 9–14; first published in Robert Osterhoudt, ed., The Philosophy of Sport: A Collection of Essays (Charles C. Thomas, 1973), pp. 48–64; see also Bernard Suits, The Grasshopper: Games, Life and Utopia (University of Toronto Press, 1978).
records.text:
> I believe that we are now in a position to define lusory attitude: the knowing acceptance of constitutive rules just so the activity made possible by such acceptance can occur.
>
> — Bernard Suits, "The Elements of Sport", p. 13

> Playing a game is the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles.
>
> — Bernard Suits, "The Elements of Sport", p. 14

Suits, a philosopher, says every game has four elements: a goal, the means allowed for reaching it, rules that ban the more efficient means, and the lusory attitude (from the Latin ludus, game). A runner could cut across the infield but doesn't, only because the rules say so; outside a game, obeying a rule just because it is a rule would look irrational. The attitude is what turns pointless obstacles into a game. Suits works the idea out at length in The Grasshopper (1978).

See also: [suits](/cards/suits)

records.title: 4X: explore, expand, exploit, exterminate
records.description: 4X names the strategy genre in which one player grows an empire across a map by exploring, expanding, exploiting and exterminating.
records.source: Alan Emrich, "MicroProse' Strategic Space Opera Is Rated XXXX!: A Revealing Sneak Preview," Computer Gaming World, no. 110 (September 1993), p. 92.
records.text:
> I give MOO a XXXX rating because it features the essential four X's of any good strategic conquest game: EXplore, EXpand, EXploit and EXterminate.
>
> — Alan Emrich, "MicroProse' Strategic Space Opera Is Rated XXXX!", Computer Gaming World no. 110, p. 92

The name comes from Alan Emrich's September 1993 preview of Master of Orion in Computer Gaming World, where a joke rating of XXXX stood for the four verbs; "4X" became the genre's name. Civilization (1991) is the best-known example. In a 4X game the map is land waiting to be claimed and worked, and success is measured by territory and output. All four verbs are things done to the map and to the people already on it.

See also: [four x](/mechanics/four-x) · [fog of war and exploration](/mechanics/fog-of-war-and-exploration) · [tech tree and unlocks](/mechanics/tech-tree-and-unlocks) · [resource conversion](/mechanics/resource-conversion) · [meier](/cards/meier) · [wark](/cards/wark)

records.title: Fog of war
records.description: Fog of war is the uncertainty of not knowing what is happening beyond what you can see, and in games, a map that stays hidden until your units reveal it.
records.source: Carl von Clausewitz, On War (1832), trans. J. J. Graham (London, 1873; Project Gutenberg eBook #1946), Book I, chapter III, "The Genius for War."
records.text:
> War is the province of uncertainty: three-fourths of those things upon which action in War must be calculated, are hidden more or less in the clouds of great uncertainty.
>
> — Carl von Clausewitz, *On War, trans. J. J. Graham, Book I, chapter III, "The Genius for War"*, Book I, ch. III

The phrase is usually traced to the Prussian general Carl von Clausewitz, whose On War (1832) compares war's uncertainty to clouds, twilight and fog, though he did not use the exact words "fog of war." Strategy games turned the idea into a rule: the whole map exists from the start, but each player sees only what their units can see, and places they have left may show old information. Knowing becomes a resource you spend effort to get, and different players see different versions of the same world.

See also: [fog of war and exploration](/mechanics/fog-of-war-and-exploration) · [four x](/mechanics/four-x)

records.title: Player characters and NPCs
records.description: A player character is controlled by a person; a non-player character (NPC) is run by the game itself or by its referee.
records.text: The terms come from tabletop role-playing games such as Dungeons & Dragons, where each player runs one character and the game master plays everyone else: shopkeepers, guards, villains. In video games, NPCs are usually run by scripts and simple decision rules, and since about 2023 some studios have shown NPCs that hold open conversations through large language models. Around 2018 "NPC" also became an online insult for a person said to have no thoughts of their own. In a game about AI, who counts as a player and who is an NPC is itself a design choice.

records.title: The core loop
records.description: The core loop is the short cycle of actions a player repeats most often, which the rest of the game is built on.
records.source: Unity Technologies, "Core Game Loop," Unity Glossary, accessed November 23, 2026, https://unity.com/glossary/core-game-loop
records.text:
> A core game loop is the repeatable cycle of actions a player performs most often in a game. It typically involves a challenge, a player action, and feedback or a reward that encourages the player to continue.
>
> — Unity Technologies, "Core Game Loop" (glossary), https://unity.com/glossary/core-game-loop

The core loop is an industry term, not an academic one. In a farming game the loop is plant, harvest, sell, then plant more; in a 4X game it is the turn: scout, settle, build, fight. Levels, upgrades and unlocks are layered on top of the loop to keep it fresh. Because the loop is what players do hundreds of times, it is where a game's rules are felt most.

See also: [four x](/mechanics/four-x) · [growth and upkeep](/mechanics/growth-and-upkeep) · [resource conversion](/mechanics/resource-conversion)

records.title: Idle and incremental (clicker) games
records.description: In an idle or incremental game, numbers grow, first by clicking and then by automation, and the game keeps running when you stop playing.
records.source: Adam Rogers, "The Way the World Ends: Not with a Bang But a Paperclip," Wired, October 21, 2017 (as cited on the Frank Lantz card); "Incremental game," Wikipedia, accessed November 23, 2026, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incremental_game
records.text:
> I thought, in a game like this, where the whole point is that you're in pursuit of maximizing a particular arbitrary quantity, it would be so funny if you were an AI and making paperclips. That game would design itself, I thought.
>
> — Frank Lantz, quoted in Adam Rogers, Wired, October 21, 2017

Incremental games such as Progress Quest (2002), Cookie Clicker (2013) and Universal Paperclips (2017) start with a click that adds one to a counter. You spend the count on machines that click for you, then on machines that build machines, and the numbers grow exponentially, often while you are away. Ian Bogost's Cow Clicker (2010) satirized Facebook social games by reducing them to clicking a cow. Frank Lantz saw that a game about maximizing one arbitrary number already models an AI with one goal, which is why Universal Paperclips casts the player as that AI.

See also: [lantz](/cards/lantz) · [bogost](/cards/bogost) · [automate this](/mechanics/automate-this) · [come back later](/mechanics/come-back-later)

records.title: Ludology vs narratology
records.description: The ludology debate asked whether games should be studied as stories or as systems of rules in their own right.
records.source: Gonzalo Frasca, "Simulation versus Narrative: Introduction to Ludology," in Mark J. P. Wolf and Bernard Perron, eds., The Video Game Theory Reader (Routledge, 2003); quotations from the author's pre-publication manuscript, https://www.cs.oswego.edu/~alex/teaching/csc430/readings/VGT_final.pdf, manuscript p. 1; Jesper Juul, "A Clash between Game and Narrative," paper presented at the Digital Arts and Culture conference, Bergen, November 1998, https://www.jesperjuul.net/text/clash_between_game_and_narrative.html; Jesper Juul, Half-Real: Video Games between Real Rules and Fictional Worlds (MIT Press, 2005), p. 1.
records.text:
> Ludology can be defined as a discipline that studies games in general, and video games in particular.
>
> — Gonzalo Frasca, "Simulation versus Narrative: Introduction to Ludology", manuscript p. 1

> computer games and narratives are very different phenomena
>
> — Jesper Juul, "A Clash between Game and Narrative" (1998), https://www.jesperjuul.net/text/clash_between_game_and_narrative.html

> To play a video game is therefore to interact with real rules while imagining a fictional world, and a video game is a set of rules as well as a fictional world.
>
> — Jesper Juul, *Half-Real*, p. 1

Around 1998–2003, scholars such as Gonzalo Frasca, Jesper Juul and Espen Aarseth argued against treating video games as a kind of film or novel; they called the study of games' own structures and rules ludology, from the Latin ludus. Frasca wrote in 1999 that game studies lacked its own discipline and so borrowed tools from literary and film theory. Frasca himself called the picture of the ludologist as simply against narrative "quite a simplification" (manuscript p. 1). The debate settled into Juul's view that a game is both real rules and a fictional world.

See also: [juul](/cards/juul)

records.title: Serious games and persuasive games
records.description: Serious games are made mainly to teach, train or inform rather than to amuse, and persuasive games are made to argue a point through their rules.
records.source: Clark C. Abt, Serious Games (Viking, 1970); Ian Bogost, Persuasive Games: The Expressive Power of Videogames (MIT Press, 2007); Gonzalo Frasca, "Simulation versus Narrative: Introduction to Ludology," in Mark J. P. Wolf and Bernard Perron, eds., The Video Game Theory Reader (Routledge, 2003); quotations from the author's pre-publication manuscript, https://www.cs.oswego.edu/~alex/teaching/csc430/readings/VGT_final.pdf, manuscript p. 4.
records.text:
> Gaming literacy will some day make players aware that games are not free of ideological content and certainly advergames will play a role in this education because they have a clear agenda.
>
> — Gonzalo Frasca, "Simulation versus Narrative: Introduction to Ludology", manuscript p. 4

Clark Abt's book Serious Games (1970) gave the name to games with an explicit educational purpose that are not played mainly for fun, including military and policy simulations. Ian Bogost's Persuasive Games (2007) argues that games can make claims about how the world works through the processes they make players carry out, which he calls procedural rhetoric, and looks at politics, advertising and education. Frasca points out that advertising games have an open agenda, and that the same is true, less openly, of any game.

See also: [bogost](/cards/bogost) · [flanagan](/cards/flanagan)

records.title: Simulation as argument
records.description: A simulation models how a system behaves, and the rules a designer puts in or leaves out make a claim about that system.
records.source: Gonzalo Frasca, "Simulation versus Narrative: Introduction to Ludology," in Mark J. P. Wolf and Bernard Perron, eds., The Video Game Theory Reader (Routledge, 2003); quotations from the author's pre-publication manuscript, https://www.cs.oswego.edu/~alex/teaching/csc430/readings/VGT_final.pdf, manuscript pp. 3, 9; Tristan Donovan, "The Replay Interviews: Will Wright," Gamasutra (Game Developer), May 23, 2011, https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/the-replay-interviews-will-wright
records.text:
> to simulate is to model a (source) system through a different system which maintains to somebody some of the behaviors of the original system
>
> — Gonzalo Frasca, "Simulation versus Narrative: Introduction to Ludology", manuscript p. 3

> In the Sim City example, the designer could convey his ideology by adding or leaving out manipulation rules that deal with, say, public transportation, racial issues or ecology.
>
> — Gonzalo Frasca, "Simulation versus Narrative: Introduction to Ludology", manuscript p. 9

> But I always wanted it to be much more open-ended, more of a toy.
>
> — Will Wright, on SimCity, "The Replay Interviews: Will Wright," interview by Tristan Donovan, Gamasutra, May 23, 2011

Frasca contrasts simulation with narrative: a photograph shows a plane, but a flight simulator models how it flies and crashes. Will Wright's SimCity (1989) began as a toy with no winning or losing, built on Jay Forrester's urban-dynamics models, and The Sims (2000) did the same for households. Even with no goal, Frasca argues, a simulation carries a point of view through its rules: which causes it includes, which it leaves out, and how they are calculated. A city simulation without public transport, or a household simulation without rent, says something about cities and households.

See also: [bogost](/cards/bogost) · [wark](/cards/wark) · [zoning](/mechanics/zoning)

records.title: What is a game?
records.description: A game is a system of rules in which players take part in an artificial conflict that ends in a measurable outcome.
records.source: Katie Salen and Eric Zimmerman, Rules of Play: Game Design Fundamentals (MIT Press, 2003), p. 96, as quoted in Jesper Juul, "The Game, the Player, the World: Looking for a Heart of Gameness" (2003); Sid Meier, GDC 2012, as reported by Leigh Alexander, Game Developer (Gamasutra), March 7, 2012.
records.text:
> A game is a system in which players engage in an artificial conflict, defined by rules, that results in a quantifiable outcome.
>
> — Katie Salen and Eric Zimmerman, Rules of Play, as quoted in Jesper Juul, "The Game, the Player, the World" (2003), p. 96

> Games are a series of interesting decisions.
>
> — Sid Meier, *GDC 2012, as reported by Leigh Alexander, Game Developer*, March 7, 2012

Salen and Zimmerman's definition has five parts: a system, players, an artificial conflict, rules that limit what players can do, and an outcome that can be counted, such as a win, a loss or a score. Sid Meier, the designer of Civilization, defines a good game from the player's side: a decision is interesting when there is no obvious right answer and the choice changes what comes next. Open-ended toys such as SimCity sit at the edge of these definitions because they have no set outcome.

See also: [salen zimmerman](/cards/salen-zimmerman) · [meier](/cards/meier)

records.title: Critical play
records.description: Critical play means playing a game fully while staying aware of what it is doing to you and what values it carries.
records.source: Mary Flanagan, interview, American Journal of Play 15, no. 2 (2023), p. 127; Mary Flanagan, Critical Play: Radical Game Design (MIT Press, 2009).
records.text:
> Critical play is simultaneously about full engagement and full awareness. It takes practice.
>
> — Mary Flanagan, *interview, American Journal of Play 15, no. 2 (2023)*, p. 127

Mary Flanagan, an artist and game designer, uses "critical play" for both playing and making games that question their own assumptions. Her book Critical Play: Radical Game Design (MIT Press, 2009) traces it through games made by artists and activists. It asks for immersion and reflection at once, and she treats it as a skill that improves with practice.

See also: [flanagan](/cards/flanagan) · [community center or joja](/mechanics/community-center-or-joja)

records.title: ACID
records.description: The four guarantees a relational database makes about every transaction: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
records.text:
**The four guarantees a relational database makes about every transaction: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.**

## In plain terms

Take a Pokémon trade. Ash sends Pikachu to Misty: Pikachu's owner changes from Ash to Misty, and the trade is logged. That's several changes that have to succeed or fail together, a [transaction](transaction.md).

- **Atomicity:** all or nothing. If the power cuts out midway, Pikachu doesn't vanish from Ash's team without landing on Misty's.
- **Consistency:** every rule holds afterward. If a trainer can carry at most six Pokémon, a trade that would give Misty a seventh is refused.
- **Isolation:** two trades running at once don't collide. Ash can't trade the same Pikachu to Misty and to Brock in the same second.
- **Durability:** once the trade is confirmed, a crash won't undo it.

A database that keeps all four is "ACID-compliant." Many NoSQL systems relax one or more of them, often consistency, so that data can be spread across many machines.

## In the readings

Dourish defines the four properties with a bank transfer (section "Processing Relational Data"), then contrasts the "ACID regime," whose canonical example is bank accounts, with Facebook's photographs, where "consistency demands are low," and notes that ACID is hard to maintain in decentralized systems (section "Shifting Materialities"). Hasan: "The value of RDBMS began to be seen against the acronym ACID," and making databases "ACID-compliant" let information retrieval "happen selectively" (p. 143).

## See also

[Transaction](transaction.md) · [Transaction log](transaction-log.md) · [Relational database](relational-database.md) · [Document database](document-database.md)

records.title: API
records.description: A doorway through which one program asks another for data or actions, using fixed requests and getting structured replies, usually in JSON.
records.text:
**A doorway through which one program asks another for data or actions, using fixed requests and getting structured replies, usually in JSON.**

## In plain terms

Apps rarely let outsiders reach their database directly. Instead they publish an API: a set of requests they'll answer. Ask a places API for cafés near a point and it returns a list of place records. Ask Spotify's Web API for a playlist and it returns the playlist with its tracks.

An API is a [view](view.md) with rules. It decides which fields you see (a place's name and rating, but not internal notes), how many requests you can make, and what you're allowed to change. It shows the shape of the data (which entities, which attributes, which relations) without saying how the data is stored. Reading API documentation is one of the best ways to see how a company models the world.

## See also

[JSON](json.md) · [View](view.md) · [Permissions](permissions.md) · [Query](query.md) · [Data independence](data-independence.md)

records.title: Attribute
records.description: One property of an entity, stored as a column: a place's name, a track's length, a parcel's owner.
records.text:
**One property of an entity, stored as a column: a place's name, a track's length, a parcel's owner.**

## In plain terms

Each attribute has a name and a [data type](data-type.md) (text, number, date, true/false), and sometimes rules: it's required, or it must come from a list. Different tools use different words for the same idea: *column* in a database table, *field* in a form or a document, *property* in JSON and many APIs, *attribute* in database design.

A medical history form's blanks are attributes: name, date of birth, "maiden name," "husband's name." Deciding the attributes decides what the record can say. If there is no attribute for something, the system can't store it, however much it matters to the person.

## In the readings

Star's medical history form (p. 384) is an argument about attributes: blanks for "maiden name" and "husband's name," and no place to name any other partner to call in an emergency.

## See also

[Entity](entity.md) · [Value](value.md) · [Data type](data-type.md) · [Constraint](constraint.md) · [Form](form.md) · Pairing: the form and its others

records.title: Audit trail
records.description: A log kept to show who changed what, when, and sometimes why, so changes can be checked later.
records.text:
**A log kept to show who changed what, when, and sometimes why, so changes can be checked later.**

## In plain terms

A [transaction log](transaction-log.md) may exist for the machine (crash recovery, copying data between servers). An audit trail exists for people: auditors, courts, supervisors, and the person the record describes. Each entry records the old value, the new value, who made the change, and when:

```
2026-09-28 10:14  operator_17  owner_name  "R. Kumar" -> "R. Kumer"
2026-09-28 11:02  verifier_03  status      "submitted" -> "error"
```

Systems where records carry legal or financial weight (banking, medical records, land registries) keep audit trails because the current record alone can't prove it was changed properly.

An audit trail is also a map of [invisible work](invisible-work.md): every correction, reversal, and override shows up in it, including the ones the final record doesn't show.

## In the readings

Hasan reports that once a Bhoomi application became a dispute, there was "no accountability mechanism" to track when it would come up for hearing (p. 155).

## See also

[Transaction log](transaction-log.md) · [Permissions](permissions.md) · [Workflow state](workflow-state.md) · [Invisible work](invisible-work.md) · [Single source of truth](single-source-of-truth.md) · Pairing: the log

records.title: Constraint
records.description: A rule the database enforces on its data: this field is required, this value must be unique, this one must come from a fixed list.
records.text:
**A rule the database enforces on its data: this field is required, this value must be unique, this one must come from a fixed list.**

## In plain terms

Constraints are the schema's rules made binding. The common ones:

- `NOT NULL`: required. The field can't be left empty.
- `UNIQUE`: no two rows may share this value (an email address, a survey number).
- `CHECK`: the value must pass a test, such as `rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5`.
- `PRIMARY KEY` and `FOREIGN KEY`: identities must be unique and pointers must lead somewhere real.

```sql
CREATE TABLE applications (
  application_id  int PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_name      text NOT NULL,
  status          text NOT NULL
    CHECK (status IN ('submitted', 'approved', 'error', 'dispute'))
);
```

A constraint protects the data from mistakes. It also decides in advance what counts as valid. The red asterisk on a form is a `NOT NULL`; the dropdown with no "other" is a `CHECK`. Whatever the constraints don't allow, the system can't record.

## See also

[Schema](schema.md) · [Null](null.md) · [Controlled vocabulary](controlled-vocabulary.md) · [Form](form.md) · [Data type](data-type.md) · Pairing: the form and its others

records.title: Controlled vocabulary
records.description: A fixed list of allowed terms for a field, so everyone uses the same word for the same thing.
records.text:
**A fixed list of allowed terms for a field, so everyone uses the same word for the same thing.**

## In plain terms

Instead of letting people type anything into "category," the system offers a list: café, bakery, bookstore. Instead of free-text genres, a set of approved ones. Controlled vocabularies make data countable and searchable ("all cafés near 50 Church Street") and stop "Cafe," "café," and "coffee shop" from splitting one category into three.

The cost: someone chose the list, and things that don't fit get forced into the nearest box or into "Other." Medical coding systems such as the International Classification of Diseases are enormous controlled vocabularies, and each revision is a negotiation over what exists.

A vocabulary can be enforced with a `CHECK` [constraint](constraint.md), or kept as its own table of terms that other rows point to. The second way makes adding a term a new row rather than a change to the structure.

## In the readings

Star describes a committee working on the International Classification of Diseases trying to define the "moment of life" for birth certificates (p. 385). Jones asks researchers to "Categorize the categorizing practices" of the people they study (p. 161).

## See also

[Constraint](constraint.md) · [Tag](tag.md) · [Master narrative](master-narrative.md) · [Form](form.md) · [Schema migration](schema-migration.md) · Pairing: recategorize · Pairing: the form and its others

records.title: CRUD
records.description: Create, Read, Update, Delete: the four basic things any system does to records.
records.text:
**Create, Read, Update, Delete: the four basic things any system does to records.**

## In plain terms

Nearly every feature of every app is one of the four. Posting is Create; scrolling is Read; editing a profile is Update; taking a song off a playlist is Delete. In SQL they're `INSERT`, `SELECT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE`.

The questions that matter socially usually hide in the U and the D. Who can update a record? Who can delete one? Is a delete an erasure, or a "deleted" flag while the row stays? Does an update overwrite the old value, or keep it in a history? These are design decisions, and they're where power in a system tends to sit.

## In the readings

Hasan's Bhoomi case turns on Update and Delete. After an operator entered the wrong name, the application left her login and she could no longer edit it, and deleting an application at the office level "was not an option any more" (p. 154).

## See also

[Permissions](permissions.md) · [Workflow state](workflow-state.md) · [Audit trail](audit-trail.md) · [Query](query.md) · [Record](record.md) · Pairing: who can update?

records.title: Data independence
records.description: The separation that lets you use a database without knowing how or where its data is physically stored.
records.text:
**The separation that lets you use a database without knowing how or where its data is physically stored.**

## In plain terms

In older systems, getting data meant knowing its path through the machine: which file, which record, which pointer to follow. Change the storage and every program that used it broke. E. F. Codd made independence a central goal of the relational model: users and programs ask for data by what it is ("all cafés rated above 4"), and the database works out where it lives and how to fetch it.

Designers distinguish *physical* data independence (the storage can change without affecting the tables people see) from *logical* data independence (the tables can be reorganized without breaking every [view](view.md) and app built on them). The first is well achieved in practice; the second only partly.

It's also what makes many interfaces to the same data possible: the app, the website, the export, and an analyst's query all read the same tables without knowing how they're stored.

## In the readings

Hasan describes the relational model bringing an interface for the "casual user," independent "from the structure of the data on the disk" (p. 142), in contrast to earlier systems where data could be reached "only by following a tree-like hierarchy" (p. 135). Dourish notes that the relational model was motivated in part by a stronger separation between the abstract data model and its machine-specific representation (section "Alternatives to the Relational Model").

## See also

[Relational database](relational-database.md) · [Hierarchical database](hierarchical-database.md) · [View](view.md) · [API](api.md) · [Schema](schema.md)

records.title: Data model
records.description: The basic shape a database uses to represent anything at all: tables, trees, networks, documents, or key-value pairs.
records.text:
**The basic shape a database uses to represent anything at all: tables, trees, networks, documents, or key-value pairs.**

## In plain terms

Before any particular schema there's a choice of kind. The [relational](relational-database.md) model says everything is tables of rows. The [hierarchical](hierarchical-database.md) model says everything is a tree of parents and children. The [document](document-database.md) model says everything is a nested document. The [key-value](key-value-store.md) model says everything is a label with a value attached.

Each is general enough to represent almost anything, but not equally easily. A family tree fits a hierarchy. Students and courses (a [many-to-many](many-to-many.md) relation) fit tables. A place with a variable set of opening hours, photos, and reviews fits a document. The data model is the deepest structural choice and the hardest to change.

"Data model" is also used more loosely for one particular design ("our data model has listeners, playlists, and tracks"). Context tells you which sense is meant.

## In the readings

Dourish compares the relational model with hierarchical, network, and attribute-value models (section "Alternatives to the Relational Model") and argues that each carries different commitments about what can be represented and done.

## See also

[Relational database](relational-database.md) · [Hierarchical database](hierarchical-database.md) · [Network database](network-database.md) · [Document database](document-database.md) · [Key-value store](key-value-store.md) · [Schema](schema.md) · Pairing: tables and documents

records.title: Data type
records.description: The kind of value a column may hold: text, whole number, decimal, date, true/false, and so on.
records.text:
**The kind of value a column may hold: text, whole number, decimal, date, true/false, and so on.**

## In plain terms

Types let the database do the right thing with a value: sort dates as dates (not alphabetically), add up numbers, reject "next Tuesday" in a date column. Choosing types is part of designing the [schema](schema.md), and each choice has consequences. A phone number stored as a number loses its leading zero. A name field limited to 30 characters cuts off long names. A yes/no column for a question with more than two answers forces people into one of two.

## In the readings

Dourish includes "the types of data (such as numbers, dates, and text items)" in his definition of a schema (section "The Materialities of Relational Data").

## See also

[Attribute](attribute.md) · [Value](value.md) · [Schema](schema.md) · [Constraint](constraint.md)

records.title: Database
records.description: An organized collection of data, kept by software that lets many people add to it, change it, and ask questions of it without breaking it.
records.text:
**An organized collection of data, kept by software that lets many people add to it, change it, and ask questions of it without breaking it.**

## In plain terms

The word names two things at once: the data (the collection of records) and the software that manages it (a database management system, or DBMS, such as Postgres or MongoDB). The software is what makes it more than a pile of files. It enforces the structure, lets many people work at the same time, answers questions (queries), and keeps the data consistent when something fails halfway through a change.

Almost every app you use sits on one. Search Google Maps for coffee near 50 Church Street and the pins are records pulled from a database of places. A Spotify playlist, a course roster, and Karnataka's Bhoomi land records are databases too. The app is the interface; the database is what's underneath.

Every database commits to a [data model](data-model.md): tables (relational), trees (hierarchical), documents, or key-value pairs. That choice shapes which questions are easy to ask and which are hard.

## In the readings

Manovich uses "database" at two levels: the computer-science sense, where he names hierarchical, network, relational, and object-oriented models (p. 81), and a cultural form that represents the world "as a list of items" (p. 85). Dourish argues that the technical differences between kinds of database shape what they can represent. Hasan's history centers on one kind, the relational database management system (RDBMS).

## See also

[Table](table.md) · [Schema](schema.md) · [Data model](data-model.md) · [Relational database](relational-database.md) · [Spreadsheet](spreadsheet.md)

records.title: Document database
records.description: A database that stores each record as a self-contained, nested document (usually JSON-like) rather than as rows spread across tables.
records.text:
**A database that stores each record as a self-contained, nested document (usually JSON-like) rather than as rows spread across tables.**

## In plain terms

Instead of splitting a place across a places table, an opening-hours table, and a photos table, a document database stores the place as one document with its hours and photo list nested inside. Read one document and you have everything about that place, with no joins.

Documents in the same collection don't have to share the same fields: one place can have a "menu" field and another not. That makes it easy to start and to change shape over time. The costs: information embedded in many documents is duplicated (change a chain's logo and you update it everywhere it was copied), and questions that cut across documents ("every place this person has reviewed") are harder than in a relational database.

The rule of thumb is that data read together is stored together. Deciding what counts as "together" is the same [granularity](granularity.md) question relational designers face, answered from the other direction.

Examples: [MongoDB](mongodb.md), Couchbase, Google's Firestore.

## In the readings

Dourish groups these systems among the "NoSQL" databases, which tend to be organized around objects rather than relations (sections "Data without Relations" and "Granularity").

## See also

[MongoDB](mongodb.md) · [JSON](json.md) · [Relational database](relational-database.md) · [Key-value store](key-value-store.md) · [Granularity](granularity.md) · Pairing: tables and documents

records.title: Entity
records.description: A kind of thing the database keeps track of: a place, a track, a person, a land parcel.
records.text:
**A kind of thing the database keeps track of: a place, a track, a person, a land parcel.**

## In plain terms

Designing a database starts with naming the entities: what kinds of things exist in this world, as far as the system is concerned? For a music app: tracks, artists, albums, playlists, listeners. For a land registry: parcels, owners, applications, officials. Each entity usually becomes a [table](table.md), and each instance of it (this track, this parcel) becomes a [record](record.md).

Choosing the entities is already an argument about the world. Is a household an entity, or only the individuals in it? Is a room a thing in its own right, or part of a house? Whatever isn't named as an entity can appear only as an [attribute](attribute.md) of something else, or not at all.

## In the readings

Hasan glosses entities as "pieces of information about the real world," such as ledgers of land records, and describes database administrators working out the relations between them from the paper registers they were digitizing (pp. 141–142).

## See also

[Table](table.md) · [Attribute](attribute.md) · [Entity-relationship diagram](entity-relationship-diagram.md) · [Granularity](granularity.md) · Pairing: what is a row?

records.title: Entity-relationship diagram
records.description: Boxes for kinds of things, lines for relations (Peter Chen, 1976); Hasan's database administrators drew them by hand (p. 142)
records.text:
- Boxes for kinds of things, lines for relations (Peter Chen, 1976)
- Hasan's database administrators drew them by hand (p. 142)

**A drawing of a database's entities as boxes and their relations as lines, used to design the structure before building it.**

## In plain terms

Each box is an [entity](entity.md), with its [attributes](attribute.md) listed inside. Each line is a relation, marked to show whether it's one-to-one, [one-to-many](one-to-many.md), or [many-to-many](many-to-many.md). The notation goes back to Peter Chen's 1976 paper. Designers sketch one before writing any `CREATE TABLE`, and reading one is the fastest way to see what a system thinks exists.

A playlist app in miniature (read `1 ── *` as "one to many"):

```
ARTIST 1 ── * TRACK * ── * PLAYLIST * ── 1 LISTENER
```

## In the readings

Hasan's database administrators at India's National Informatics Centre drew "entity-relation (or E-R)" diagrams with paper and pen, working out the relations from the ledgers and registers they were digitizing, which engineers called "domain knowledge" (p. 142).

## See also

[Entity](entity.md) · [Attribute](attribute.md) · [One-to-many](one-to-many.md) · [Many-to-many](many-to-many.md) · [Schema](schema.md)

records.title: First normal form (1NF)
records.description: One value per cell: no lists inside a field, and no repeating columns like Type 1, Type 2, Type 3.
records.text:
**One value per cell: no lists inside a field, and no repeating columns like Type 1, Type 2, Type 3.**

## In plain terms

A Pokémon has one or more types. There are two tempting ways to fit that into one table, and both break first normal form.

A list in one cell: the LL's spreadsheet of Pokémon puts all of a Pokémon's abilities in one text cell ("Blaze, Solar Power" for Charizard), and you can't easily count, sort, or search the parts of it. Airtable's Types column looks like a list too (`[Fire, Flying]`), but Airtable keeps each link as a proper relation behind the scenes.

Repeating columns: Type 1, Type 2. That works until something has three. In the LL's Pokédex data, five Pokémon list three types (Arctozolt: Flying, Electric, Ice), so a two-column sheet silently drops one.

The 1NF fix is a table where each row holds one fact, one Pokémon paired with one type:

```
pokemon_types
pokemon      type
-----------  --------
Charizard    Fire
Charizard    Flying
Arctozolt    Flying
Arctozolt    Electric
Arctozolt    Ice
```

Now "how many Fire types are there?" is a simple count (80 in the LL's data), and a fourth type needs a new row, not a new column. This is a [join table](join-table.md).

## See also

[Normalization](normalization.md) · [Second normal form](second-normal-form.md) · [Third normal form](third-normal-form.md) · [Many-to-many](many-to-many.md) · [Join table](join-table.md)

records.title: Foreign key
records.description: A column that holds another table's primary key, pointing from this row to a row somewhere else.
records.text:
**A column that holds another table's primary key, pointing from this row to a row somewhere else.**

## In plain terms

A tracks table has an `artist_id` column; each value in it is the ID of a row in the artists table. That column is a foreign key. It's how relations between entities are stored: not by copying the artist's name into every track, but by pointing to the one artist row.

```sql
CREATE TABLE tracks (
  track_id   text PRIMARY KEY,
  title      text NOT NULL,
  artist_id  text REFERENCES artists(artist_id)
);
```

The database can enforce the pointer (this is called referential integrity). It won't let you add a track whose `artist_id` doesn't exist, or delete an artist who still has tracks, unless you've said what should happen to them.

## In the readings

Hasan describes the shift from older systems, which used pointers "enforcing some sort of referential link between entities," to tables whose connections could be expressed "whenever desired" (p. 141). A foreign key is how that works: the connection is stored as an ordinary value and followed when a query asks for it.

## See also

[Primary key](primary-key.md) · [Join](join.md) · [One-to-many](one-to-many.md) · [Constraint](constraint.md) · [Normalization](normalization.md)

records.title: Form
records.description: The screen or paper where a person enters one record: the front door of a table, showing its schema as questions.
records.text:
**The screen or paper where a person enters one record: the front door of a table, showing its schema as questions.**

## In plain terms

Every blank on a form is a column. Every required asterisk is a `NOT NULL`. Every dropdown is a [controlled vocabulary](controlled-vocabulary.md). Every "Submit" is an INSERT. A course registration, a medical intake sheet, a streaming-service sign-up, and a land-record application are all forms in front of tables.

Forms are where the schema meets people. The person filling one in has to translate their situation into the form's categories. When it doesn't fit (no box for their kind of household, a name longer than the field allows, an address with no street number), they make something up, leave it blank, or write in the margin, where it never reaches the database.

## In the readings

Star's medical history form has blanks for "maiden name" and "husband's name" and no place for any other partner (p. 384). On p. 385, statisticians argue over how to define the "moment of life" for birth certificates, and the distinctions drawn by the designers of death certificates fail to match how attending doctors see the world. In Hasan's Bhoomi case, the error enters through an application keyed in by an operator (p. 154).
