records.title: Granularity
records.description: What size of thing counts as one unit in the database: a house or a room, a song or an album, a household or a person.
records.text:
**What size of thing counts as one unit in the database: a house or a room, a song or an album, a household or a person.**

## In plain terms

Every table decides what one row is. A property register might have one row per house; a heating system, one row per room. Neither is wrong, but each makes some questions easy and others awkward. Granularity also means how fine the detail is: a play count per song per day, or every single play with its timestamp.

In practice a designer rarely has to pick only one level. A houses table and a rooms table, linked [one-to-many](one-to-many.md), let you reason about both. The harder choices are about what gets recorded at all: if the system stores only the household, the individuals in it are invisible to every query.

## In the readings

Dourish's example (section "Granularity"): if a house must always be represented as a collection of rooms, it becomes easier to reason about heating systems "but harder to reason about property rights." In the same section he notes that SQL commands act at three scales: UPDATE on values, INSERT on rows, CREATE TABLE on tables.

## See also

[Entity](entity.md) · [Record](record.md) · [One-to-many](one-to-many.md) · [Schema](schema.md) · [Provisionality](provisionality.md) · Pairing: what is a row?

records.title: Hierarchical database
records.description: A database that stores data as a tree: each record has one parent and may have many children.
records.text:
**A database that stores data as a tree: each record has one parent and may have many children.**

## In plain terms

Picture the folders on a computer: drives contain folders, folders contain subfolders, subfolders contain files. A hierarchical database works the same way: a state contains districts, districts contain villages, villages contain parcels. To reach a record you follow the path down from the top. IBM's IMS, built in the late 1960s, is the classic example, and it's still in use at large banks.

Trees are fast and natural when the world has one clear hierarchy. They struggle when it doesn't: a parcel held by owners in two villages, a song on many playlists. Anything with more than one parent has to be copied or awkwardly cross-linked, and the questions that are easy to ask depend on where you start in the tree.

Computer folders, XML files, and the nesting inside a [JSON](json.md) document are all hierarchical, which is why document and hierarchical databases have a family resemblance.

## In the readings

Hasan: before Codd, data could be reached "only by following a tree-like hierarchy" of the system, Folder-File-Data (p. 135). Dourish describes the tree model (section "Alternatives to the Relational Model") and notes that hierarchical and network databases don't separate structure from content (section "The Materialities of Relational Data"). Jones's paper hanging files, holding manila folders (p. 153), are a physical hierarchy: each folder sits in one place.

## See also

[Network database](network-database.md) · [Relational database](relational-database.md) · [Document database](document-database.md) · [Tag](tag.md) · [Data independence](data-independence.md) · Pairing: recategorize · Pairing: tables and documents

records.title: Index
records.description: An extra structure a database keeps so it can find rows by a column's value without reading the whole table.
records.text:
**An extra structure a database keeps so it can find rows by a column's value without reading the whole table.**

## In plain terms

Like the index of a book: to find every mention of Codd you don't read every page. A database index on `category` lets it jump straight to all the cafés. Primary keys are indexed automatically; designers add indexes on the columns people search by most.

```sql
CREATE INDEX places_by_category ON places (category);
```

Indexes speed up reading and slightly slow down writing (every insert has to update the index too), so they're a trade-off chosen around the questions people are expected to ask. Most use a structure called a B-tree, invented in the early 1970s.

## In the readings

Hasan explains indexes built on primary keys and the B-tree, and cites the argument that without indexing, relational databases might have stayed too inefficient to succeed (p. 142).

## See also

[Primary key](primary-key.md) · [Query](query.md) · [Relational database](relational-database.md)

records.title: Join
records.description: A query that combines rows from two or more tables by matching keys, so facts stored separately come back together.
records.text:
**A query that combines rows from two or more tables by matching keys, so facts stored separately come back together.**

## In plain terms

Because a relational database keeps each kind of thing in its own table, most useful answers need a join. "Show me this playlist with song titles and artist names" joins the playlist entries to tracks (on `track_id`) and tracks to artists (on `artist_id`).

```sql
SELECT e.position, t.title, a.name AS artist
FROM playlist_entries e
JOIN tracks  t ON t.track_id  = e.track_id
JOIN artists a ON a.artist_id = t.artist_id
WHERE e.playlist_id = 'road-trip'
ORDER BY e.position;
```

The result looks like one spreadsheet, but it's assembled on request and discarded afterward. The relations between tables become visible at the moment of asking.

Document databases encourage storing related data together (embedding) so fewer joins are needed. MongoDB has a join-like `$lookup` step for when you need one.

## See also

[Join table](join-table.md) · [Foreign key](foreign-key.md) · [Query](query.md) · [SQL](sql.md) · [View](view.md) · Pairing: the list and the narrative

records.title: Join table
records.description: A table whose rows are connections between two other tables
records.text:
- A table whose rows are connections between two other tables

**A table whose rows are connections between two other tables. It stores a many-to-many relation, often with facts about each connection.**

## In plain terms

A playlist can be modeled as three tables: playlists, tracks, and playlist entries. Each entry row says: this track is on this playlist, at this position, added at this time. (Spotify's public Web API, for example, returns each playlist item with the track and the time it was added.)

```sql
CREATE TABLE playlist_entries (
  playlist_id  text REFERENCES playlists(playlist_id),
  position     int,
  track_id     text REFERENCES tracks(track_id),
  added_at     timestamp,
  PRIMARY KEY (playlist_id, position)
);
```

The interesting data often lives in the join table itself. A Premiere timeline can be modeled the same way: the clips sit in the project (one table), and the timeline is a list of entries, each pointing to a clip, with an in-point, an out-point, and a place in the sequence. The same clip can be used ten times.

This is one way to see Manovich's database/narrative opposition under the hood. The collection is one table; the narrative is another table, an ordered list of references into the first. Both are stored.

## In the readings

Manovich names Premiere's "project" as the database at the center of new media design, from which a sequence is built (p. 89).

## See also

[Many-to-many](many-to-many.md) · [Join](join.md) · [Foreign key](foreign-key.md) · [Paradigm and syntagm](paradigm-and-syntagm.md) · [Tag](tag.md) · Pairing: the list and the narrative

records.title: JSON
records.description: A plain-text format for structured data: named fields, lists, and objects nested inside objects.
records.text:
**A plain-text format for structured data: named fields, lists, and objects nested inside objects.**

## In plain terms

JSON is how most [APIs](api.md) send data and how document databases like [MongoDB](mongodb.md) represent records. It has a few building blocks: objects in `{ }` with named fields, lists in `[ ]`, text in quotes, numbers, `true`/`false`, and `null`. Objects can nest, so one record can hold its own sub-records.

A place record, simplified, in the style of what a places API returns:

```json
{
  "id": "place_123",
  "name": "Blue Door Café",
  "address": "Church St, Cambridge, MA",
  "location": { "lat": 42.3746, "lng": -71.1206 },
  "types": ["cafe", "bakery"],
  "openingHours": [
    { "day": "Mon", "open": "07:00", "close": "18:00" },
    { "day": "Tue", "open": "07:00", "close": "18:00" }
  ],
  "rating": 4.5
}
```

Notice what a spreadsheet row can't easily hold: a list of types, a nested location, a varying number of opening-hours entries. In a relational database each of those would become its own table, linked by keys.

## See also

[Document database](document-database.md) · [MongoDB](mongodb.md) · [API](api.md) · [Hierarchical database](hierarchical-database.md) · Pairing: tables and documents

records.title: Key-value store
records.description: The simplest kind of database: a giant lookup table where each key maps to one value, retrieved only by its key.
records.text:
**The simplest kind of database: a giant lookup table where each key maps to one value, retrieved only by its key.**

## In plain terms

Give it a key (`listener:4812:last_played`) and it gives back a value (a track ID, a block of JSON, a number). No tables, no joins, no searching by content: you have to know the key. In exchange, key-value stores are very fast and easy to spread across many machines, which is why they're used for caches, login sessions, shopping carts, and settings.

Examples: Redis, Amazon DynamoDB in its simplest use, and the `localStorage` built into every web browser.

## In the readings

Dourish describes "attribute-value" or "key-value" systems, where each object carries an unstructured set of keys and values, such as an "owner" key holding his own name (section "Data without Relations"). In such systems, finding a value "without knowing the key" is often inefficient or impossible.

## See also

[Document database](document-database.md) · [Data model](data-model.md) · [Primary key](primary-key.md) · Pairing: tables and documents

records.title: Many-to-many
records.description: A relation where records on both sides can connect to many on the other: a song can be on many playlists, and a playlist holds many songs.
records.text:
**A relation where records on both sides can connect to many on the other: a song can be on many playlists, and a playlist holds many songs.**

## In plain terms

One foreign key can't store this, because neither side can hold a single pointer. The standard solution is a third table, a [join table](join-table.md), with one row per connection.

Other examples: students and courses; photos and the people tagged in them; research notes and the categories they belong to. The last is the difference between folders and tags. A folder system is one-to-many: each file lives in exactly one folder. [Tags](tag.md) are many-to-many: one note can carry many tags, and each tag gathers many notes.

## In the readings

Jones notes that software such as Atlas.ti lets you create "nonexclusive folders" (p. 156), folders an item can belong to more than one of. That is a many-to-many relation.

## See also

[Join table](join-table.md) · [Tag](tag.md) · [One-to-many](one-to-many.md) · [Foreign key](foreign-key.md) · Pairing: the list and the narrative · Pairing: recategorize

records.title: MongoDB
records.description: A widely used document database that stores records as JSON-like documents (BSON), with flexible, nested structure.
records.text:
**A widely used document database that stores records as JSON-like documents (BSON), with flexible, nested structure.**

## In plain terms

MongoDB, first released in 2009, groups documents into collections (roughly where a relational database has tables). Documents are stored as BSON, a binary form of JSON that adds types such as dates. By default the documents in a collection don't have to share fields, though you can add validation rules.

MongoDB encourages embedding: put what you read together into one document, such as a playlist with its tracks listed inside it. It can join across collections with its `$lookup` step, and supports multi-document transactions, but its design pushes you toward documents shaped around how the app will use them.

```json
{
  "_id": "road-trip",
  "name": "Road trip",
  "owner": "listener_4812",
  "tracks": [
    { "trackId": "t1", "title": "Song A", "artist": "Artist X", "addedAt": "2026-09-01" },
    { "trackId": "t2", "title": "Song B", "artist": "Artist Y", "addedAt": "2026-09-03" }
  ]
}
```

Compare the relational version: playlists, tracks, artists, and a playlist-entries [join table](join-table.md). Here the artist's name is copied into every playlist that includes the song.

## In the readings

Dourish lists MongoDB among the platforms that "abandon the relational/transactional model altogether" (section "Shifting Materialities"). He was writing in 2014; MongoDB added multi-document transactions in 2018.

## See also

[Document database](document-database.md) · [JSON](json.md) · [Postgres](postgres.md) · [Join](join.md) · Pairing: tables and documents

records.title: Network database
records.description: An older kind of database where records are linked directly to one another by stored pointers, allowing many parents and arbitrary connections.
records.text:
**An older kind of database where records are linked directly to one another by stored pointers, allowing many parents and arbitrary connections.**

## In plain terms

The network model, standardized around 1970 (the CODASYL specifications), loosened the tree: a record could have many parents and many kinds of links. Programs moved through the data by following pointers from record to record, a bit like following links on the web.

It was flexible but brittle. The links were built into the stored data, so programs depended on its layout, and a question that needed an unplanned path meant writing new code. The relational model's answer was to drop stored pointers and connect records through key values when a query asks. Graph databases today (Neo4j, for example) bring back first-class links, with modern query languages.

## In the readings

Dourish describes network models with typed links such as "IS-A" and "HAS-A" (section "Alternatives to the Relational Model"). Hasan contrasts pointers "enforcing some sort of referential link between entities" with tables that express connections when desired (p. 141).

## See also

[Hierarchical database](hierarchical-database.md) · [Relational database](relational-database.md) · [Foreign key](foreign-key.md) · [Data model](data-model.md)

records.title: Normalization
records.description: Storing each fact in one place, and pointing to it everywhere else
records.text:
- Storing each fact in one place, and pointing to it everywhere else

**Organizing tables so each fact is stored in exactly one place, and everything else refers to it by key.**

## In plain terms

In an unnormalized playlist spreadsheet, the artist's name appears on every track row. Rename the artist and you have to find and fix every copy; miss one and the data disagrees with itself. Normalization splits that out: an artists table holds the name once, and tracks point to it with `artist_id`. Fix the spelling in one row and every playlist, search, and page that shows the artist is corrected at once.

Designers describe degrees of normalization as "normal forms" (first, second, third, and beyond), each ruling out a particular kind of duplication: [first](first-normal-form.md), [second](second-normal-form.md), and [third](third-normal-form.md) each have their own entry, with Pokémon examples. Sometimes they deliberately denormalize, keeping copies for speed, and accept the work of keeping the copies in sync.

Normalization makes correcting a mistake technically easy. It doesn't settle who is allowed to make the correction, or what proof they need. Those are questions of [permissions](permissions.md) and [workflow](workflow-state.md).

## In the readings

Hasan's Bhoomi case (pp. 153–155) is a good test. A wrong name could be fixed with one change to one record, yet the correction runs through a dispute process and a court order. Ask where that burden comes from: the data structure, or who controls the record?

## See also

[First normal form](first-normal-form.md) · [Second normal form](second-normal-form.md) · [Third normal form](third-normal-form.md) · [Single source of truth](single-source-of-truth.md) · [Foreign key](foreign-key.md) · [Permissions](permissions.md) · [Workflow state](workflow-state.md) · [Spreadsheet](spreadsheet.md) · Pairing: who can update?

records.title: NoSQL
records.description: Databases that drop the relational model; Dourish's title
records.text: - Databases that drop the relational model; Dourish's title

records.title: Null
records.description: The marker for a missing or unknown value: not zero, not empty text, but nothing recorded.
records.text:
**The marker for a missing or unknown value: not zero, not empty text, but nothing recorded.**

## In plain terms

If a place has no phone number on file, its phone column is NULL. Null means "we don't know" or "doesn't apply," and databases treat it specially. NULL isn't equal to anything, not even another NULL, so `WHERE phone = NULL` finds nothing; you have to write `WHERE phone IS NULL`.

A column can forbid nulls with `NOT NULL`, which makes the field required. That choice is a claim about the world: every person has a date of birth, but not every person has a husband. When a form insists on a value that doesn't apply, people invent one ("N/A," "unknown," a placeholder date), and the database fills up with values that look real and aren't.

Nulls also appear whenever the structure grows: add a new column to a table of a million places and a million nulls appear with it.

## See also

[Constraint](constraint.md) · [Value](value.md) · [Form](form.md) · [Attribute](attribute.md) · [Schema migration](schema-migration.md) · Pairing: the form and its others

records.title: One-to-many
records.description: A relation where one record on one side connects to many on the other: one house has many rooms; one artist has many tracks.
records.text:
**A relation where one record on one side connects to many on the other: one house has many rooms; one artist has many tracks.**

## In plain terms

It's stored by putting a [foreign key](foreign-key.md) on the "many" side: each room row carries its `house_id`. One house, many rooms, each room in exactly one house. Other examples: one Premiere project has many clips; one land parcel has many applications filed against it over the years.

Dourish's houses-and-rooms example can sound like a forced choice between two units. The usual design keeps both:

```sql
CREATE TABLE houses (
  house_id  int PRIMARY KEY,
  address   text
);
CREATE TABLE rooms (
  room_id   int PRIMARY KEY,
  house_id  int REFERENCES houses(house_id),
  name      text,
  radiator  boolean
);
```

Property rights attach to houses; heating attaches to rooms. The choice doesn't vanish, though. Someone still decides what counts as a room, and whatever the system never records (who sleeps where) stays out of reach of every query.

## In the readings

Dourish, section "Granularity": representing a house as a collection of rooms makes heating easier to reason about and property rights harder.

## See also

[Many-to-many](many-to-many.md) · [Foreign key](foreign-key.md) · [Granularity](granularity.md) · [Entity-relationship diagram](entity-relationship-diagram.md) · Pairing: what is a row?

records.title: Permissions
records.description: The rules about who may create, read, update, or delete which records.
records.text:
**The rules about who may create, read, update, or delete which records.**

## In plain terms

Databases and apps grant rights to roles: a viewer can read, an editor can update, an administrator can delete and change the structure. In SQL:

```sql
GRANT SELECT ON places TO analyst;
GRANT SELECT, UPDATE ON applications TO verifier;
```

In an app it's the difference between a playlist you can edit and one you can only follow.

Permissions encode an organization's hierarchy of trust. They decide who can fix a mistake and who has to ask someone else to fix it. A system can make a correction technically trivial (one UPDATE) and still make it institutionally hard, because the person who notices the error isn't allowed to change it.

## In the readings

In Hasan's account, the Bhoomi operator who made an error couldn't correct it once the application had left her login; the owner then had to prove the correct version through a dispute process (pp. 154–155).

## See also

[CRUD](crud.md) · [Workflow state](workflow-state.md) · [Audit trail](audit-trail.md) · [Normalization](normalization.md) · [API](api.md) · Pairing: who can update?

records.title: Postgres
records.description: A widely used, open-source relational database that stores data in tables and is queried with SQL.
records.text:
**A widely used, open-source relational database that stores data in tables and is queried with SQL.**

## In plain terms

Postgres began as a research project at the University of California, Berkeley, in the 1980s, gained SQL in the mid-1990s, and was renamed PostgreSQL. It's free, runs almost anywhere, and is known for following the SQL standard closely and enforcing constraints strictly. Many hosted database services (Supabase, for one) are Postgres underneath.

Though relational at heart, Postgres can also store JSON in a column (the `jsonb` type) and query inside it, so one system can hold strict tables and flexible documents side by side. Extensions add more: PostGIS adds geographic queries such as "places within 500 meters of 50 Church Street":

```sql
SELECT name FROM places
WHERE ST_DWithin(geog, ST_MakePoint(-71.1206, 42.3746)::geography, 500);
```

## See also

[Relational database](relational-database.md) · [SQL](sql.md) · [MongoDB](mongodb.md) · [JSON](json.md) · Pairing: tables and documents

records.title: Primary key
records.description: The value that identifies one row and no other
records.text:
- The value that identifies one row and no other

**The column (or columns) whose value uniquely identifies each row in a table, so no row is ever mistaken for another.**

## In plain terms

Names aren't unique: there are many cafés called "Blue Door," and many farmers with the same name. So tables give every row an identifier: a number, a code, or a long random string. A Google Maps place has a place ID; a Spotify track has a track ID; a land parcel in Hasan's Karnataka has a survey number. The database refuses to store two rows with the same primary key.

Keys are what other tables point to. A playlist entry doesn't copy a song's title; it stores the track's ID. That lets one record be referred to from many places without being duplicated.

A good key never changes. If the key is something meaningful (a name, an address) and the thing changes, every reference to it breaks, which is why most systems use IDs that mean nothing.

## In the readings

Hasan describes indexes built from "unique identifiers (or the 'primary key' in database language)" for every record (p. 142).

## See also

[Foreign key](foreign-key.md) · [Index](database-index.md) · [Record](record.md) · [Join](join.md)

records.title: Query
records.description: A question put to a database in a form it can answer: which rows, which columns, in what order.
records.text:
**A question put to a database in a form it can answer: which rows, which columns, in what order.**

## In plain terms

"Cafés within a few blocks of 50 Church Street, best-rated first" is a query in English. In SQL, against a table of places with coordinates, it might look like this (the numbers are an approximate box around Church Street):

```sql
SELECT name, category, rating
FROM places
WHERE category = 'cafe'
  AND latitude  BETWEEN 42.372 AND 42.377
  AND longitude BETWEEN -71.124 AND -71.117
ORDER BY rating DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Every search box, filter, map view, and "recommended for you" list runs a query somebody wrote, often with your inputs dropped into it. A query can only find what the schema records: if the table has no "wheelchair accessible" column, no query can answer that question.

Queries read; they don't change the data (reading is the R in [CRUD](crud.md)). Commands that change it (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) are more properly called statements, though people often call everything a query.

## See also

[SQL](sql.md) · [View](view.md) · [Join](join.md) · [CRUD](crud.md) · [Index](database-index.md)

records.title: Record
records.description: One instance of an entity: a single row holding the values for one place, one track, one land parcel.
records.text:
**One instance of an entity: a single row holding the values for one place, one track, one land parcel.**

## In plain terms

If the table is "places," a record is one place: this café, with its name, address, coordinates, and category. Records are what a database accumulates. A busy system adds millions of them without changing its structure at all.

The word matters outside databases too. In an office, "the record" is the official version of something, and correcting it can be a legal process. The two senses meet in systems like land registries, where a row *is* the legal record.

## In the readings

Dourish notes that SQL's INSERT acts at the scale of the row, which he calls a relation (section "Granularity"). In Hasan's Bhoomi case, one wrong name in one record sends a landholder into a dispute process that ends in a court order (pp. 153–155).

## See also

[Table](table.md) · [Value](value.md) · [Primary key](primary-key.md) · [Granularity](granularity.md) · [CRUD](crud.md) · Pairing: what is a row?

records.title: Relational database
records.description: Tables of rows and columns, linked by keys, queried with SQL
records.text:
- Tables of rows and columns, linked by keys, queried with SQL

**A database that stores everything in tables of rows and columns, links the tables with keys, and is queried with SQL.**

## In plain terms

The relational model was proposed by E. F. Codd at IBM in a 1970 paper and became the dominant way to store structured data from the 1980s on. The idea: represent everything as [tables](table.md); connect them by storing [keys](foreign-key.md) rather than pointers; answer questions by combining tables on request ([joins](join.md)), on a mathematical foundation that makes queries predictable.

Strengths: each fact stored once ([normalization](normalization.md)), enforced rules ([constraints](constraint.md)), reliable changes ([transactions](transaction.md)), and the ability to answer questions nobody planned for when the tables were designed. Costs: the [schema](schema.md) has to be designed up front and is expensive to change, and data with a varying, nested shape has to be split across many tables.

Examples: [Postgres](postgres.md), MySQL, SQLite (built into every iPhone and Android phone), Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server.

## In the readings

Hasan's chapter is in part a history of the RDBMS in Indian government; he dates Codd's invention to 1973 (p. 123), though Codd's founding paper appeared in 1970. Dourish explains the model (section "Data Formats and the Relational Model") and why its separation of schema from content matters (section "The Materialities of Relational Data").

## See also

[Table](table.md) · [SQL](sql.md) · [Normalization](normalization.md) · [Transaction](transaction.md) · [Postgres](postgres.md) · [Document database](document-database.md) · Pairing: tables and documents

records.title: Schema
records.description: The declared structure of a database: tables, columns, rules
records.text:
- The declared structure of a database: tables, columns, rules

**The declared structure of a database: its tables, their columns, each column's type, and the rules the data must follow.**

## In plain terms

The schema is the design; the data is what fills it. A set of `CREATE TABLE` statements is a schema written down. A [form](form.md) is a schema shown to the person filling it in.

Separating the two gives the relational database its character. Content changes constantly (add a million places, update a rating, delete a café that closed) and the schema stays still. Changing the schema itself, with a new column or a different idea of what a row is, is a bigger event, and old data may not fit the new shape (see [schema migration](schema-migration.md)).

Document databases are called "schemaless" or schema-flexible, but the structure doesn't disappear. It moves into the application code and into the habits of whoever writes the documents.

## In the readings

Dourish (section "The Materialities of Relational Data"): the schema "defines the set of tables and the columns," must be set up before data is entered, and is often "difficult or impossible to change once data entry has begun." Hierarchical and network databases, he notes, do not "reify structure" separately in this way.

## See also

[Data model](data-model.md) · [Schema migration](schema-migration.md) · [Provisionality](provisionality.md) · [Constraint](constraint.md) · [Form](form.md)

records.title: Schema migration
records.description: A change to a database's structure (adding, removing, or redefining tables and columns), applied to a database that already holds data.
records.text:
**A change to a database's structure (adding, removing, or redefining tables and columns), applied to a database that already holds data.**

## In plain terms

Adding a row costs nothing structurally. Changing the structure is different: every existing row has to be made to fit the new shape.

```sql
ALTER TABLE places ADD COLUMN wheelchair_accessible boolean;
```

That one is easy to run, but every existing place now has [NULL](null.md) in the new column: unknown, until someone goes and finds out. Harder migrations change what a row means: splitting one `owner_name` into several owners, turning a single `category` into many [tags](tag.md), deciding a household record should become one record per person. The old data may not hold the information the new structure asks for, and every app built on the old structure breaks until it's rewritten.

Teams write migrations as small numbered scripts, apply them in order, and keep them under version control, because the history of the structure matters as much as the history of the data.

## In the readings

This is the practical side of Dourish's point that the database is provisional "only with limits" (section "The Materialities of Relational Data"). Jones describes the same inertia in a filing system: "Succumbing to the inertia of the filing system, I effectively gave up on the project" (p. 157).

records.title: Second normal form (2NF)
records.description: In a table whose key has two parts, every other column must depend on both parts, not just one.
records.text:
**In a table whose key has two parts, every other column must depend on both parts, not just one.**

## In plain terms

Which Pokémon can learn which moves is a many-to-many relation, stored in a join table whose key is the pair (Pokémon, move). Suppose we also put the move's type in that table:

```
pokemon_moves
pokemon      move          move_type
-----------  ------------  ---------
Charmander   Flamethrower  Fire
Vulpix       Flamethrower  Fire
Arcanine     Flamethrower  Fire
Snorlax      Flamethrower  Fire
```

Flamethrower is a Fire move no matter who learns it. Its type depends on the move alone, only half of the key, so the same fact is written once per Pokémon that knows it. If it ever changed, every copy would have to change.

The 2NF fix moves that column to the table where it belongs:

```
moves                       pokemon_moves
move          type          pokemon      move
------------  ----          -----------  ------------
Flamethrower  Fire          Charmander   Flamethrower
Surf          Water         Vulpix       Flamethrower
```

The join table keeps only what depends on the pair. A column that does depend on both parts (the level at which this Pokémon learns this move, say) can stay.

## See also

[Normalization](normalization.md) · [First normal form](first-normal-form.md) · [Third normal form](third-normal-form.md) · [Primary key](primary-key.md) · [Join table](join-table.md)

records.title: Single source of truth
records.description: The one place where a fact is officially kept, which every other copy or view defers to.
records.text:
**The one place where a fact is officially kept, which every other copy or view defers to.**

## In plain terms

When the same fact lives in two places (a spreadsheet and a database, a paper ledger and a digital record), the two will eventually disagree, and someone has to decide which one wins. Naming a single source of truth settles that in advance: the land registry, not the photocopy; the database, not last month's export.

Inside a database, [normalization](normalization.md) is how you get a single source of truth for each fact. Across an organization, it's a policy decision.

The phrase hides a question worth asking: truth for whom? The official record can be wrong, and when it is, the person it describes may have to bring evidence from outside the system to change it.

## In the readings

In Hasan's account, when a digital land record is found to be wrong, the law makes it the owner's job to prove that a correct version exists, "irrespective of the source of the error," and owners are sent back to paper records to do it (pp. 153–154).

## See also

[Normalization](normalization.md) · [Permissions](permissions.md) · [Audit trail](audit-trail.md) · [Excess](excess.md) · Pairing: who can update?

records.title: Spreadsheet
records.description: A grid of cells you can type anything into. It looks like a database table but enforces almost nothing, and one sheet can't express relations between different kinds of things.
records.text:
**A grid of cells you can type anything into. It looks like a database table but enforces almost nothing, and one sheet can't express relations between different kinds of things.**

## In plain terms

A spreadsheet (Excel, Google Sheets) and a database table look alike: rows and columns. The difference is in what they enforce. In a sheet, any cell can hold anything: a date in the price column, a note typed across a row, two artists crammed into one cell with a comma. A database table has a [schema](schema.md): every value in a column has the same type and obeys the same rules.

The bigger difference is relations. Keep a playlist in one sheet and you repeat the artist's name on every row for that artist's songs, and the album's release year on every track from the album. Spell the artist two ways and the sheet has no idea they're the same person. A relational database splits this into separate tables (tracks, artists, albums) and links them with [keys](foreign-key.md), so each fact is stored once.

So a single sheet is closer to one table, or to the flattened result of a [join](join.md), than to a relational database. Many real databases start life as a spreadsheet that got too big to trust.

## See also

[Table](table.md) · [Normalization](normalization.md) · [Relational database](relational-database.md) · [Foreign key](foreign-key.md) · [Single source of truth](single-source-of-truth.md) · Pairing: what is a row?

records.title: SQL
records.description: The standard language for defining, changing, and asking questions of relational databases.
records.text:
**The standard language for defining, changing, and asking questions of relational databases.**

## In plain terms

SQL (said "sequel" or "S-Q-L") came out of IBM research in the 1970s. It's now an international standard, used, with local dialects, by nearly every relational database: [Postgres](postgres.md), MySQL, SQLite, Oracle, and others. It's declarative: you describe the result you want, and the database works out how to get it.

It works at several scales:

- `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`: the structure (the [schema](schema.md)).
- `INSERT`, `DELETE`: whole rows.
- `UPDATE`: values inside rows.
- `SELECT`: reading, with `WHERE`, `JOIN`, `ORDER BY`, `GROUP BY`.
- `GRANT`, `REVOKE`: who may do what.

## In the readings

Dourish's title, "No SQL," names the family of databases that set the relational model aside; he calls SQL "the canonical way" of programming relational databases (section "Shifting Materialities"). In his granularity section he matches commands to scales: UPDATE acts on values, INSERT on rows, CREATE TABLE on tables.

## See also

[Query](query.md) · [Relational database](relational-database.md) · [Postgres](postgres.md) · [CRUD](crud.md) · [Schema](schema.md)

records.title: Table
records.description: A set of records of one kind, laid out as rows (one per thing) and columns (one per property).
records.text:
**A set of records of one kind, laid out as rows (one per thing) and columns (one per property).**

## In plain terms

A table holds one kind of thing: places, tracks, clips, land parcels, people. Each row is one of those things; each column is one fact about it. In the relational model a table is formally called a *relation*, which is where "relational" comes from (not from the links *between* tables, though there are those too).

```sql
CREATE TABLE places (
  place_id   text PRIMARY KEY,
  name       text NOT NULL,
  category   text,
  latitude   numeric,
  longitude  numeric
);
```

The design question for every table is which [entity](entity.md) it represents and what counts as one instance of it. A database is usually many tables, linked by [keys](primary-key.md).

## In the readings

Dourish describes relational data as organized into tables, where each column encodes "information of a particular sort" and each row expresses a relation between data items (section "Data Formats and the Relational Model"). Hasan: with Codd's model, the table became the storage format, "as opposed to a tree-like or hierarchical structure" (p. 123).

## See also

[Entity](entity.md) · [Record](record.md) · [Attribute](attribute.md) · [Schema](schema.md) · [Relational database](relational-database.md) · Pairing: what is a row?

records.title: Tag
records.description: A label attached to a record, where one record can carry many labels and each label gathers many records.
records.text:
**A label attached to a record, where one record can carry many labels and each label gathers many records.**

## In plain terms

Folders make you choose: a file sits in one folder. Tags don't: a field note about a magic show can be tagged *performance*, *colonial archive*, and *audience* all at once. In database terms, folders are [one-to-many](one-to-many.md) and tags are [many-to-many](many-to-many.md), stored with a [join table](join-table.md):

```
notes          tags             note_tags
-----          ----             ---------
n1  "..."      t1 performance   n1  t1
n2  "..."      t2 audience      n1  t2
                                n2  t2
```

Tags can be free (anyone types anything, as with hashtags) or controlled (chosen from a fixed list). Free tags are flexible and messy; controlled tags are consistent and limiting. Many systems end up with both.

Recategorizing with tags is cheap: add or remove a row in the join table. With folders it means moving things. With a new column in the schema, it means a [migration](schema-migration.md).

## In the readings

Jones works with paper hanging files, and notes that software such as Atlas.ti allows "nonexclusive folders" (p. 156). Dourish's example of large, informal storage is a collection of "'tagged'" photographs (section "Shifting Materialities").

## See also

[Many-to-many](many-to-many.md) · [Join table](join-table.md) · [Controlled vocabulary](controlled-vocabulary.md) · [Hierarchical database](hierarchical-database.md) · [Schema migration](schema-migration.md) · Pairing: recategorize

records.title: Third normal form (3NF)
records.description: No column depends on another non-key column: a fact about a type is stored with the type, not copied onto every Pokémon.
records.text:
**No column depends on another non-key column: a fact about a type is stored with the type, not copied onto every Pokémon.**

## In plain terms

Fire takes double damage from Water, Ground, and Rock. That's a fact about Fire, not about Charmander. A table that stores it on each Pokémon breaks third normal form:

```
pokemon
name        type  weak_to
----------  ----  --------------------
Charmander  Fire  Water, Ground, Rock
Vulpix      Fire  Water, Ground, Rock
Growlithe   Fire  Water, Ground, Rock
```

`weak_to` depends on `type`, which depends on the Pokémon: a chain, not a direct link. The same weaknesses are written 80 times, once per Fire Pokémon, and a correction has to reach all 80.

The 3NF fix stores the weaknesses once, with the type, and has each Pokémon point to its type by key:

```
types                          pokemon
id  name  weak_to              name        type_id
--  ----  -------------------  ----------  -------
10  Fire  Water, Ground, Rock  Charmander  10
                               Vulpix      10
```

(Fully normalized, `weak_to` becomes its own table too, one row per pair of types.)

Airtable's Pokémon table shows a "Double Damage From" column on every Pokémon, but it's a lookup: it reads the linked Types record and stores nothing itself, so a mistake is fixed once, on the type. The LL's copy has one. Every type's "Double Damage From" repeats its "Double Damage Against," so Fire looks weak to Bug, Steel, Grass, and Ice, the types it beats. One edit to the Fire record would fix all 80 Fire Pokémon.

## See also

[Normalization](normalization.md) · [First normal form](first-normal-form.md) · [Second normal form](second-normal-form.md) · [Foreign key](foreign-key.md) · [Single source of truth](single-source-of-truth.md)

records.title: Transaction
records.description: A group of changes the database treats as one: either all of them happen or none do.
records.text:
**A group of changes the database treats as one: either all of them happen or none do.**

## In plain terms

Moving money between accounts means subtracting from one and adding to the other. If the system crashes between the two steps, the money exists twice or not at all. A transaction wraps both steps so they succeed or fail together:

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 'A';
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 'B';
COMMIT;
```

Relational databases guarantee four properties for transactions, abbreviated [ACID](acid.md):

- **Atomicity:** all or nothing.
- **Consistency:** the data moves from one valid state to another, and the rules are never left broken.
- **Isolation:** transactions running at the same time don't see each other's half-finished work.
- **Durability:** once committed, a change survives a crash.

Not to be confused with a transaction in the everyday sense (a purchase), though a purchase is usually recorded as one.

## In the readings

Dourish uses the bank transfer to explain transactions and ACID (section "Processing Relational Data"), then argues that these guarantees shaped hardware, benchmarks, and business arrangements around them (section "The Materialities of Relational Data Processing").

## See also

[ACID](acid.md) · [Transaction log](transaction-log.md) · [Relational database](relational-database.md) · [CRUD](crud.md)

records.title: Transaction log
records.description: A record of every action in a system, in order; Star: "I know of no one who has analyzed transaction logs to their own satisfaction" (p. 384)
records.text:
- A record of every action in a system, in order
- Star: "I know of no one who has analyzed transaction logs to their own satisfaction" (p. 384)

**An append-only record of every change or action in a system, in the order it happened.**

## In plain terms

A table usually shows the current *state*: this playlist has these 20 songs. A log shows *events*: added song A at 9:02, removed song B at 9:05, moved song C to the top at 9:06. You can rebuild the state from the events, but not the events from the state.

Logs are append-only: new entries go at the end and old ones aren't edited. Databases keep internal logs so they can recover from crashes; apps keep logs of clicks, plays, searches, and edits. A listening history is a log; so is a bank statement.

The difference matters for analysis. The current record says what's true now. The log says how it got that way: who did what, and what was tried and undone.

## In the readings

Star (p. 384) notes the promise of "almost ready-made 'fieldnotes'" in transaction logs and e-mail archives, and adds that she knows of no one who has analyzed transaction logs to their own satisfaction.

## See also

[Audit trail](audit-trail.md) · [Transaction](transaction.md) · [CRUD](crud.md) · [Invisible work](invisible-work.md) · Pairing: the log

records.title: Value
records.description: The single piece of data in one cell: this row's entry in this column.
records.text:
**The single piece of data in one cell: this row's entry in this column.**

## In plain terms

"Blue Door Café," 2026-09-28, 4.5, true. A value sits where a [record](record.md) (row) crosses an [attribute](attribute.md) (column). It's the smallest thing a relational database usually edits: fixing a misspelled name is an UPDATE on one value.

```sql
UPDATE places SET name = 'Blue Door Café' WHERE place_id = 'p_123';
```

Values come with [types](data-type.md): a date column holds dates, not the word "yesterday." Some values are free text; some must come from a fixed list (a [controlled vocabulary](controlled-vocabulary.md)); some are references to rows in other tables ([foreign keys](foreign-key.md)). The absence of a value is its own thing: [null](null.md).

## In the readings

Dourish names data values as the smallest of the relational database's three scales, the one SQL's UPDATE acts on (section "Granularity").

## See also

[Record](record.md) · [Attribute](attribute.md) · [Data type](data-type.md) · [Null](null.md) · [Controlled vocabulary](controlled-vocabulary.md)

records.title: View
records.description: A saved query that behaves like a table; more broadly, any one way of presenting data that lives underneath.
records.text:
**A saved query that behaves like a table; more broadly, any one way of presenting data that lives underneath.**

## In plain terms

In SQL a view is a named query:

```sql
CREATE VIEW cafes_near_church_st AS
SELECT name, rating FROM places
WHERE category = 'cafe'
  AND latitude  BETWEEN 42.372 AND 42.377
  AND longitude BETWEEN -71.124 AND -71.117;
```

You read from it like a table, but it stores nothing; it's recomputed from the underlying tables each time. Views let different people see different slices of the same data, or the same data arranged differently, without copying it.

The same idea runs through every app. A Spotify playlist on your phone, the same playlist on the web, its export as a spreadsheet, and the shuffled order you hear are four views of the same rows. A Google Maps place shows up as a pin, a card, a search result, and a line in your saved list. Change the underlying record and every view changes with it.

## In the readings

Manovich: in new media "the content of the work and the interface become separate," which makes possible "different interfaces to the same material" (p. 86).

## See also

[Query](query.md) · [API](api.md) · [Data independence](data-independence.md) · [Paradigm and syntagm](paradigm-and-syntagm.md) · [Form](form.md) · Pairing: the list and the narrative

records.title: Workflow state
records.description: A field recording where a record is in a process (submitted, approved, disputed), with rules about which moves are allowed and who may make them.
records.text:
**A field recording where a record is in a process (submitted, approved, disputed), with rules about which moves are allowed and who may make them.**

## In plain terms

Many records aren't only facts but cases moving through steps. An application goes from submitted to verified to approved; an order goes from placed to shipped to delivered. Systems store this as a status field and enforce which transitions are allowed and who may make them:

```
submitted ──(verifier)──> approved
submitted ──(verifier)──> error ──> dispute ──(court order)──> submitted
```

Workflow state is where a database becomes a bureaucracy. Each state has a queue, an owner, and a waiting time, and a record can get stuck in one.

## In the readings

In Hasan's Bhoomi case (p. 154), a verifier checked an application against an older paper document and marked it as an error. It left the 'mutation' flow (in Indian land administration, mutation is the process of recording a change in a land record) and went onto a 'dispute' list, needing a scanned court order to return. Once marked 'dispute,' it fell out of the system's first-in-first-out queue (p. 155).

records.text:
> Databases make the world. They do so in at least two ways. The first and more trivial of these is that the world is increasingly made up of databases, as digital technologies continue to supplement, surround, or displace other forms of record keeping. The second and more consequential way in which databases make the world, though, is that this very spread of digital forms means that we increasingly understand, talk about, think about, and describe the world as the sort of thing that can be encoded and represented in a database.
>
> — section "Introduction"
