records.text: Meta will help pay to extend and expand Vistra's existing nuclear plants in Ohio and Pennsylvania, fund two TerraPower reactors that could produce power by 2032, and back Oklo's planned nuclear campus in Pike County, Ohio, which could start as soon as 2030. Together the projects could add 6.6 GW by 2035. The TerraPower and Oklo reactors have not been built yet.

records.title: Microsoft–Brookfield renewable power deal
records.description: A May 2024 agreement for Brookfield to develop more than 10.5 GW of new renewable power for Microsoft.
records.text: The framework covers wind, solar and other carbon-free power in the US and Europe, to be delivered from 2026 to 2030. It was almost eight times larger than the biggest single corporate power deal signed before it. Individual contracts are signed project by project under the framework.

records.title: Nuclear power
records.description: Steady, low-carbon power that tech companies have started buying directly, including from a reactor being restarted for the purpose.
records.text: In 2024 Microsoft agreed to buy power from a reactor at Three Mile Island that had closed in 2019, and Google and Amazon signed deals for small modular reactors that have not been built yet.

records.title: On-site gas power for data centres
records.description: Gas turbines and engines built at or next to data centres so they can run without waiting for a grid connection.
records.text: The IEA estimates 15 to 27 GW of on-site gas power may serve data centres by 2030, mostly in the US. To be reliable, such plants need 30% to 70% more generating capacity than the load they serve. Gas turbine orders rose about 70% in 2025. Examples include xAI's plant in Southaven, Mississippi, the turbines at the Stargate campus in Abilene, Texas, and Meta's Socrates plants in Ohio.

records.title: PJM capacity auction
records.description: The yearly auction in which PJM, the grid operator for 13 states and Washington, DC, pays power plants to be available in future years.
records.text: PJM serves about 67 million people. In its auction for 2027–28 the price hit the cap of $333.44 per MW per day. In July 2026 the auction for 2028–29 again cleared at the cap, $325, and still fell 6,831 MW short of what PJM needs for reliability. PJM says large new loads such as data centres are increasingly being added to the demand forecast that sets how much power it must buy.

records.title: Socrates gas plants (Meta, Ohio)
records.description: Gas-fired power plants built on site to help power Meta's Prometheus AI cluster in New Albany, Ohio.
records.text: Socrates South had 10 gas turbines in place by March 2026, with about 139 MW of its 200 MW running by late August 2026, according to Epoch AI. Socrates North had its turbines installed by early September 2026 and was projected to run fully by late 2026. A third plant of up to 250 MW is projected for 2028.

records.title: Solar, wind and batteries
records.description: Cheap, clean power that comes and goes with the weather, unless it is paired with storage.
records.text: Companies buy renewable power to meet climate pledges, but matching it to a data centre that never sleeps is hard.

records.title: Talen–Amazon Susquehanna nuclear deal
records.description: A June 2025 deal for Talen Energy to supply up to 1,920 MW from the Susquehanna nuclear plant in Pennsylvania to Amazon's data centres.
records.text: Amazon had bought a data centre campus next to the Susquehanna plant and wanted more power straight from it, but federal regulators (FERC) rejected a plan to raise the amount sent directly. In the new deal the plant's power goes onto the regional grid run by PJM, and Talen sells it to Amazon through the grid. The contract runs to 2042 and reaches full volume by 2032. The companies also plan to look at small modular reactors and at upgrades to squeeze more power from the plant.

records.title: The electricity grid
records.description: The power plants, transmission lines and substations that deliver electricity, and the queue to connect to them.
records.text: AI data centres are adding demand faster than grids planned for. Building new lines can take a decade, which is why some companies now build or buy power plants directly.

records.title: Utilities and grid operators
records.description: The companies and agencies that decide who can connect to the electricity grid, and when.
records.text: A new data centre can wait years for a grid connection. Utilities have to balance its demand against homes and other businesses, and usually pass the cost of new power plants and lines on to customers.

records.title: xAI's Southaven gas turbine plant (Mississippi)
records.description: A gas turbine power plant in Southaven, Mississippi, just across the state line from Memphis, that powers xAI's Colossus 2.
records.text: The plant is run by MZX Tech, an xAI company now part of SpaceX. On March 10, 2026 Mississippi's environmental permit board approved 41 permanent gas turbines to replace 27 that had been running without a permit, which state regulators treated as temporary. Neighbours complain of constant noise and worry about air pollution, and the NAACP sued under the Clean Air Act. In November 2026 the board voted 6-1 to keep the permit, and a federal judge had already let the NAACP lawsuit go ahead.

records.title: 2Africa cable
records.description: A Meta-led undersea internet cable about 45,000 km long that circles Africa and links it to Europe and Asia.
records.text: 2Africa reaches 33 countries and is longer than Earth's circumference; Meta announced on November 17, 2025 that its core system was complete after nearly six years of work. It was built by a consortium of Meta with Bayobab (MTN Group), center3 (stc), CMI, Orange, Telecom Egypt, Vodafone Group and WIOCC. Cables like this carry the traffic between users and the data centres that serve AI models.

records.title: Copper
records.description: The metal in the cables, transformers, switchgear and cooling plates that power and cool data centres.
records.text: An estimated 30 to 40 percent of data-centre construction is electrical work, and all of it uses copper, from the transformers and switchgear that bring power in to the copper plates that cool chips. The bank Macquarie estimated 330,000 to 420,000 tonnes of copper will be used in data centres by 2030. In the United States, two-to-five-year waits for transformers have been a bigger bottleneck than copper itself, and new mines take at least ten years to open.

records.title: Critical minerals
records.description: Gallium, germanium, rare earths, copper, cobalt: the raw materials in chips, magnets, wires and batteries.
records.text: Their mining and refining are concentrated in a few countries, especially China, which restricted exports of gallium and germanium in 2023.

records.title: Dunant cable
records.description: Google's undersea cable across the Atlantic between Virginia Beach and Saint-Hilaire-de-Riez, France.
records.text: Google announced on February 3, 2021 that Dunant was ready for service. It carries 250 terabits per second over 12 fibre pairs, and was the first long-haul undersea cable built with that design. Google owns cables like this so that traffic between its data centres on two continents does not depend on anyone else's network.

records.title: Escondida copper mine
records.description: An open-pit copper mine in Chile's Atacama Desert, described as the world's largest.
records.text: Escondida sits about 3,100 metres up in the Antofagasta Region of Chile and produced about 1.28 million tonnes of copper in its 2024 financial year. BHP owns 57.5 percent and Rio Tinto 30 percent. Mining needs water in one of the driest places on Earth: the mine once pumped groundwater, was ordered by a court in 2024 to pay more than US$8 million in compensation over groundwater extraction, and now runs on a coastal desalination plant.

records.title: Gallium
records.description: A soft metal used to make compound semiconductor chips, LEDs and power electronics.
records.text: Gallium is not mined on its own: it is recovered as a by-product, mostly from bauxite (aluminium ore) and some zinc ores. It goes into gallium arsenide and gallium nitride chips used in electronics, LEDs, power electronics and satellites. In 2024 China produced 98 percent of the world's low-purity gallium, so Chinese export rules can squeeze supply for chipmakers everywhere.

records.title: Germanium
records.description: A semiconductor element used in fibre-optic cables, infrared optics and electronics.
records.text: Germanium is mainly recovered as a by-product of zinc processing, and also from coal fly ash. In 2023 its biggest uses were fibre optics (26 percent) and infrared optics (22 percent), with electronics and solar cells next. China is the world's largest source, which is why its export rules on germanium matter to the companies that build data networks.

records.title: Google's data centre in Canelones, Uruguay
records.description: A Google data centre redesigned to use air cooling after protests during Uruguay's 2023 drought.
records.text: Google's original design would have used up to 7.6 million litres of drinking water a day, during a drought that reached crisis levels in July 2023 and led to protests. Uruguay approved it in August 2024, and Google then committed US$850 million to the site.

records.title: Google's water use in The Dalles
records.description: A 13-month fight in Oregon over whether the public could know how much water Google's data centres use.
records.text: The city of The Dalles, Oregon, sued its local newspaper, The Oregonian, to keep Google's data-centre water use secret as a trade secret. It dropped the case in December 2022 after Google agreed to release the numbers and to publish site-level water data for all its US data centres. Google said its data centres in the city of about 15,000 people used about 274.5 million gallons (about 1 billion litres) of water in a year.

records.title: Heavy rare earth elements
records.description: A group of metals such as dysprosium and terbium used to make strong magnets.
records.text: Rare earth elements are used in magnets for electric vehicles, wind turbines, wireless technology and military equipment. Until 2023 China did 99 percent of the world's processing of heavy rare earths. Since April 2025, exporters of seven of them (samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium and yttrium) have needed a Chinese licence for every shipment.

records.title: Helium
records.description: A gas chip factories blow over wafers to cool them during etching, with no ready substitute.
records.text: Chipmakers use helium to draw heat away from silicon wafers during etching, and under current processes there is no viable replacement. The United States is the largest producer, followed by Qatar, Algeria and Russia; Qatar makes about 30 percent of the world's supply as a by-product of natural gas. South Korea imports about 65 percent of its helium from Qatar, which makes its big memory-chip makers sensitive to any disruption there.

records.title: MAREA cable
records.description: A 6,644 km undersea cable between Virginia Beach in the United States and Bilbao in Spain.
records.text: MAREA was built by Microsoft, Facebook (now Meta) and the telecom company Telxius and has been in service since April 2018, with a design capacity of 160 terabits per second. It lands at Telxius's Virginia Beach cable landing station, which also hosts the BRUSA cable and Google's Dunant cable. These cables connect the huge cluster of data centres in northern Virginia to Europe.

records.title: Ras Laffan helium shutdown
records.description: In March 2026 drone attacks during the Iran war halted gas and helium production at Qatar's Ras Laffan complex.
records.text: QatarGas halted gas production at Ras Laffan, the world's largest liquefied natural gas plant and the source of Qatar's helium, on March 2, 2026 after Iranian drone attacks, and declared force majeure two days later. Further strikes caused what the company called extensive damage that would take years to repair. Spot helium prices doubled, and about 200 specialised helium containers were stuck in the Middle East. TSMC said it did not expect a significant impact.

records.title: Red Sea cable cuts
records.description: On September 6, 2025 undersea cables in the Red Sea near Jeddah were cut, slowing internet and cloud traffic.
records.text: The internet monitor NetBlocks linked the outages to the SMW4 and IMEWE cable systems near Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, and reported degraded connections in Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, the United Arab Emirates and India. Microsoft said traffic on its Azure cloud passing through the Middle East might see increased delays as it was rerouted. Microsoft did not say what caused the cuts; cables can be damaged by ship anchors or deliberate attacks.

records.title: Spruce Pine high-purity quartz
records.description: Ultra-pure quartz from mines around Spruce Pine, North Carolina, used to make the crucibles that melt silicon for chips.
records.text: Two companies, Sibelco and The Quartz Corp, make high-purity quartz from the Spruce Pine mines. An estimated 70 to 90 percent of the crucibles used worldwide to melt polysilicon are made from it, and it also goes into solar panels and fibre-optic cables. Both companies shut down ahead of Hurricane Helene in 2024; Sibelco restarted in October 2024, showing how one small town can be a weak point for the whole chip supply chain.

records.title: Taiwan's 2021 drought
records.description: One of Taiwan's worst droughts, when water was rationed for homes and trucked in for chip factories.
records.text: In 2021, after a year when no typhoon hit the island, some of Taiwan's reservoirs fell to 10 to 15 percent of capacity. Household water was rationed while thousands of trucks carried water to the semiconductor industry, angering farmers whose water had been set aside for them. Chipmaking uses about 20 percent of Taiwan's water. Heavy rain later refilled the reservoirs.

records.title: Ukrainian neon
records.description: Neon gas purified in Ukraine and used in the lasers that print patterns onto chips.
records.text: Neon is used in the lasers for lithography, the step that carves circuit patterns onto silicon wafers. Before 2022 more than half of the world's neon came from a handful of Ukrainian companies, including Ingas in Mariupol and Cryoin in Odesa. Both stopped operating amid Russian attacks in early 2022. Chipmakers had stockpiles and other suppliers, and only about two-fifths of the neon used in chipmaking came from Russia and Ukraine.

records.title: Undersea cables
records.description: Fibre-optic cables on the ocean floor that carry almost all traffic between continents.
records.text: There are a few hundred of them. They can be cut by ship anchors or on purpose, and repair ships are few.

records.title: US 50 percent copper tariff
records.description: A US tariff of 50 percent on imported semi-finished copper products, including cables and electrical components, from August 1, 2025.
records.text: On July 30, 2025 President Trump signed a proclamation putting a 50 percent tariff on imported semi-finished copper products such as wire, rods, pipes and tubes, and on copper-heavy parts such as cables, connectors and electrical components. It took effect on August 1, 2025. Raw inputs such as copper ore, concentrates and cathodes were left out. The parts it covers are the same kinds of parts that go into data centres and power lines.

records.title: Water
records.description: Ultra-pure water to wash chips in fabs, and water evaporated to cool some data centres.
records.text: Water is local: a data centre or fab draws on the same rivers and aquifers as the town next to it, which is where disputes start.

records.title: AI Diffusion Rule
records.description: A January 2025 US rule sorting the world into three tiers for AI chip exports, cancelled before it took effect.
records.text: Issued by the Biden administration in January 2025, the rule would for the first time have limited exports of US AI chips to many countries: close allies such as Japan and South Korea faced no limits, countries such as Mexico and Portugal faced caps, and countries such as China and Russia faced the tightest controls. On May 13, 2025, days before it was due to take effect, the Trump administration rescinded it. The Commerce Department instead warned that using Huawei's Ascend AI chips anywhere in the world breaks US export rules.

records.title: America's AI Action Plan
records.description: The White House plan of July 23, 2025 for AI, with a companion order to speed permits for big data centres.
records.text: The plan, titled "Winning the AI Race," lists more than 90 federal actions under three pillars: speeding up innovation, building American AI infrastructure, and leading in international diplomacy and security. A companion executive order signed the same day, Executive Order 14318, offers loans, grants and tax incentives and faster environmental reviews for data centres needing more than 100 megawatts of new power or at least US$500 million in investment, and opens federal and military land to them. It also calls for training more electricians and HVAC technicians.

records.title: California SB 53
records.description: California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, signed September 29, 2025.
records.text: Written by State Senator Scott Wiener and signed by Governor Gavin Newsom, the law requires large developers of frontier AI models to publish how they apply safety standards and best practices. It creates a way to report critical safety incidents to the state's Office of Emergency Services, protects whistleblowers, and lets the Attorney General seek civil penalties. It also sets up CalCompute, a plan for a public computing cluster.

records.title: China's gallium and germanium export controls
records.description: Chinese licence rules from August 1, 2023, then a ban on sales to the US, for metals used in chips.
records.text: China announced on July 3, 2023 that from August 1, 2023 exporters of gallium and germanium would need licences naming the buyer, end user and use; it cited national security. In December 2024 it banned approving exports of gallium, germanium and antimony to the United States. On November 9, 2025, after a Trump-Xi meeting, China suspended that ban until November 27, 2026, while keeping the licence system.

records.title: China's rare earth export controls
records.description: Chinese licence rules on rare earths from April 2025, expanded in October 2025 to target chipmakers, then partly paused.
records.text: On April 4, 2025 China required licences to export seven heavy rare earths and magnets, in response to US tariffs. On October 9, 2025 it added five more elements, required a licence for foreign products containing 0.1 percent or more Chinese rare earths by value, and said applications linked to advanced chips (14 nm logic and below, 256-layer memory and above) would be reviewed case by case. China suspended the October measures in November 2025 and, on November 9, 2026, extended that pause to January 10, 2027; the April 2025 licences were never paused.

records.title: CHIPS Act award and US stake in Intel
records.description: A US$7.86 billion CHIPS grant to Intel in 2024, much of it turned into a government stake of nearly 10 percent in 2025.
records.text: In late November 2024 the Commerce Department finalised up to US$7.86 billion for Intel, less than the US$8.5 billion first announced. Intel had received about US$2.2 billion of it when, on August 22, 2025, the government agreed to buy US$8.9 billion of Intel stock, nearly 10 percent of the company, paid for mostly with nearly US$6 billion of grants not yet handed over. Intel says the stake is passive, with no board seats.

records.title: CHIPS Act award to TSMC Arizona
records.description: A US$6.6 billion CHIPS Act grant to TSMC for its chip factories in Arizona, finalised in November 2024.
records.text: The US Commerce Department finalised up to US$6.6 billion in direct funding for TSMC Arizona in mid-November 2024, the same amount as its April 2024 preliminary deal. The money is paid out as the company completes project milestones. It is part of the US effort to make leading-edge chips at home rather than relying only on factories in Taiwan.

records.title: Digital Omnibus delay to the EU AI Act
records.description: A 2026 EU law that pushed back the AI Act's rules for high-risk AI systems to December 2027 and August 2028.
records.text: The European Commission proposed the Digital Omnibus on AI in November 2025. The European Parliament approved it on June 16, 2026, the Council adopted it on June 29, 2026, and it entered into force on July 27, 2026 as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. Rules for standalone high-risk AI systems move from August 2, 2026 to December 2, 2027, and rules for AI built into regulated products move to August 2, 2028. It also adds a ban, from December 2, 2026, on AI systems that generate non-consensual intimate images or child sexual abuse material.

records.title: Dutch controls on chipmaking machines
records.description: Netherlands licence rules, from September 1, 2023, for exporting ASML's most advanced lithography machines.
records.text: On June 30, 2023 the Dutch government announced that from September 1, 2023, companies would need a licence to export advanced chipmaking equipment, including ASML's top DUV immersion lithography machines (the NXT:2000i and later models). It cited national security and did not name China; the move followed US pressure on allies. On September 6, 2024 the rules were widened to the older NXT:1970i and 1980i models, from September 7, 2024.

records.title: Executive order against state AI laws
records.description: Executive Order 14365 of December 11, 2025, which set up a federal task force to challenge state AI laws.
records.text: The order told the US Attorney General to create an AI Litigation Task Force within 30 days to challenge state AI laws that conflict with federal policy. States with laws the administration calls onerous could lose some federal broadband funds, and White House advisers were told to draft a national AI law that would override conflicting state laws, except on child safety. The order names a Colorado law on algorithmic discrimination as an example.

records.title: Export controls
records.description: Rules that forbid selling certain chips and chip-making machines to certain countries.
records.text: The US rules of October 2022, tightened since, limit China's access to advanced AI chips and the tools to make them. Allies, including the Netherlands and Japan, added their own.

records.title: Georgia's data-centre tax break veto
records.description: On May 7, 2024 Georgia's governor vetoed a bill to pause the state's sales-tax break for data centres.
records.text: House Bill 1192 would have paused Georgia's sales-tax exemption for building and equipping data centres for two years and set up a study of their effect on the power grid. Governor Brian Kemp vetoed it, saying companies had already made plans relying on the exemption. A 2022 University of Georgia review projected the state would give up US$307 million more in tax from 2024 to 2030 than data centres bring in, while Georgia Power said it needed new, mostly gas-fired, power plants to serve them.

records.title: Ireland's data-centre grid connection rules
records.description: Rules from Ireland's energy regulator, December 12, 2025, requiring new data centres to bring their own power.
records.text: Data centres used about 22 percent of Ireland's electricity in 2024, up from about 5 percent in 2015, and are projected to reach 31 percent by 2034. Under the Commission for Regulation of Utilities' decision, new data centres must provide generation or storage on site or nearby that matches the power they draw, and must eventually meet at least 80 percent of their yearly demand with new renewable electricity generated in Ireland. Grid operators had to publish a connection process by March 31, 2026.

records.title: Japan's controls on chipmaking equipment
records.description: Japanese licence rules for exporting 23 kinds of advanced chipmaking equipment, in force from July 23, 2023.
records.text: Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry issued the rules on May 23, 2023, and they took effect on July 23, 2023. They cover cleaning, deposition, heat treatment, lithography, etching and inspection equipment above set performance levels, and apply regardless of destination. Japan is home to major tool makers, so its rules, along with the Dutch ones, extended US limits on China's chipmaking.

records.title: Loudoun County data-centre rules
records.description: The Virginia county at the heart of Data Center Alley ended automatic approval of data centres in 2025 and paused new votes in 2026.
records.text: On March 18, 2025 Loudoun County's Board of Supervisors ended by-right data-centre development, so every new data centre needs public hearings and a board vote. On November 17, 2026 the board paused votes on data-centre and electrical-substation applications for up to 12 months, backdated to September 15, 2026, affecting about 33 applications. The county attorney had said a full moratorium would not be legal; the pause is meant to last until new planning and zoning rules are finished, expected in summer 2027.

records.title: New export rules
records.description: A government changes what can be sold to whom, overnight.
records.text: A move a government player can make: it changes every other player's supply at once.

records.title: Nvidia H200 sales to China
records.description: A January 2026 US decision to allow Nvidia H200 chip sales to China with conditions and a 25 percent cut for the government.
records.text: President Trump announced in December 2025 that H200 sales to China would be allowed with the US government taking 25 percent, and the Commerce Department published the rule in January 2026. Chips must be tested in the United States first, and shipments to China are capped at half of what goes to US customers. House documents released on November 19, 2026 showed more than 879,000 AI chips approved for Chinese companies, but Nvidia said it had stopped shipping H200s to China; analysts said Beijing had not approved large-scale imports. On November 16, 2026 Commerce issued a rule to stop Chinese companies renting Nvidia computing power from data centres in other countries.

records.title: Taiwan
records.description: The island where most of the world's most advanced chips are made, and a flashpoint between the US and China.
records.text: Some call TSMC Taiwan's "silicon shield": the idea that the world depends on its chips too much to let it be attacked. Whether that idea holds is argued over.

records.title: The CHIPS Act
records.description: A 2022 US law giving tens of billions of dollars to build chip factories in the United States.
records.text: It is industrial policy: paying to move part of the supply chain home, so that fewer of the world's chips depend on Taiwan.

records.title: The EU AI Act
records.description: A European law (2024) that sorts AI uses by risk, banning some and setting duties for others.
records.text: It sorts uses into tiers, from banned (such as social scoring) to high-risk (such as hiring) to lightly regulated, with extra rules for the largest general-purpose models.

records.title: The European Union
records.description: Passed the AI Act in 2024, the first broad law sorting AI systems by risk.
records.text: The EU has few frontier labs of its own, but a market large enough that companies everywhere follow its rules. Its power in the game is the rulebook.

records.title: The government of China
records.description: Backs its own chip industry and AI labs, and controls the export of minerals chips depend on, such as gallium and germanium.
records.text: Restricted from buying the most advanced chips and machines, China has invested in making its own, and has answered with export limits of its own on critical minerals.

records.title: The United States government
records.description: Sets export controls on chips and chip-making tools, and funds fabs at home through the CHIPS Act.
records.text: Through the Commerce Department, the US decides which advanced chips and machines may be sold to China and others. It can act on the whole supply chain at once, by rule rather than by building anything.

records.title: US chip export rules of December 2024
records.description: US rules of December 2, 2024 that restricted high-bandwidth memory and more chipmaking tools, and blacklisted 140 entities.
records.text: For the first time the US controlled exports of high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the fast memory stacked beside AI chips. The rules also covered 24 types of chipmaking equipment and three kinds of chip-design software, and added 140 entities, including Chinese chip factories, tool makers and investment companies, to the Entity List. The stated aim was to slow China's development of advanced AI with military uses.

records.title: US chip export rules of October 2022
records.description: The first sweeping US rules limiting China's access to advanced AI chips and chipmaking equipment, announced October 7, 2022.
records.text: The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security required licences to send certain advanced computing chips to China and for exports supporting supercomputers and chip factories there. Factories in China making the most advanced logic, DRAM and NAND memory chips needed licences for US equipment, and US citizens could not help such factories without one. The rules took effect on October 12 and 21, 2022, and later rules built on them.

records.title: US chip export rules of October 2023
records.description: Three US rules of October 17, 2023 that tightened the 2022 chip limits and closed ways around them.
records.text: The update changed how restricted chips are measured so that slightly weakened chips could no longer slip under the limits, and required licences for chips going to companies headquartered in China or other covered countries anywhere in the world. Licence requirements for chipmaking equipment were extended to 21 more countries under a US arms embargo, and 13 Chinese entities were added to the Entity List. The chip rule took effect on November 16, 2023.

records.title: A strike
records.description: Workers stop work to win terms, including terms about AI.
records.text: In 2023 Hollywood's writers struck for almost five months (May 2 to September 27); their new contract included rules on how studios may use AI.

records.title: Communities near data centres
records.description: The neighbours who live with a data centre's noise, water use, land use and power lines, and sometimes its tax money.
records.text: Some towns court data centres for tax revenue; others fight them over noise, water and higher power bills. Their say comes through zoning boards and local elections.

records.title: Content Moderators Union in Africa
records.description: A union of content moderators for Facebook, TikTok and ChatGPT, voted into being in Nairobi on May 1, 2023.
records.text: More than 150 current and former moderators who worked through the outsourcing firms Sama and Majorel met in Nairobi on Labour Day 2023 and voted to register the union, described as the first of its kind in Africa. They pointed to post-traumatic stress, too little mental-health care, insecure jobs and pay as low as US$1.50 an hour. The effort goes back to 2019, when a Sama worker was fired after trying to start a union.

records.title: Data Center Watch
records.description: A research group that counts US data-centre projects blocked or delayed by local opposition.
records.text: Its first report, in May 2025, found US$64 billion of US data-centre projects blocked or delayed by local, bipartisan opposition. In the second quarter of 2026 alone it counted 45 projects worth US$68 billion blocked or delayed, more than half of the new large projects it began tracking. It counts 843 opposition groups in 49 states, and has also recorded protests in Europe, Australia and South Africa.

records.title: Data workers
records.description: People paid, often by the task and often in low-wage countries, to label data, rate model answers and filter harmful content.
records.text: Chatbots learn to be helpful partly from thousands of people rating their answers. A 2023 Time investigation reported that Kenyan workers paid under $2 an hour labelled violent and abusive text to make ChatGPT safer.

records.title: Global Trade Union Alliance of Content Moderators
records.description: An alliance of content moderators' unions from nine countries, launched in Nairobi in April 2025.
records.text: Unions from Kenya, Ghana, Colombia, Poland, Turkey, the Philippines, Portugal, Tunisia and Morocco formed the alliance to press Meta, TikTok, Alphabet and Amazon over how moderators hired through contractors are treated. Its first demand was for mental-health protocols across tech supply chains, including limited exposure to harmful content, realistic quotas, round-the-clock counselling, living wages and the right to join a union.

records.title: Google AI raters laid off
records.description: In 2025 more than 200 contract workers who rated Google's Gemini and AI Overviews answers were let go.
records.text: The raters were employed by GlobalLogic, an outsourcing firm owned by Hitachi, and its subcontractors, and some earned US$28 to US$32 an hour while others doing the same job through subcontractors earned US$18 to US$22. They had been organising with the Alphabet Workers Union, which grew from under 20 members in late 2024 to about 60 by early 2025, and two filed complaints with the National Labor Relations Board. Google said they were not its employees.

records.title: Hackers
records.description: People who break into systems: for money, for a government, to prove a point, or to test the defences on purpose.
records.text: Some hackers are criminals, some work for states, and some ("red teams") are hired to attack a system so its owners can fix it. A hack is something a hacker does; the hacker is a character.

records.title: Kenyan content moderators' case against Meta
records.description: A Kenyan court case by about 185 Facebook moderators who say they lost their jobs after trying to unionise.
records.text: The moderators reviewed Facebook content in Nairobi for Sama, a contractor, and say they lost their jobs after trying to organise a union and were then blacklisted when Meta switched to another contractor, Majorel. Kenya's labour court ruled in 2023 that Meta could be sued there, and in September 2024 the Court of Appeal upheld that, rejecting Meta's argument that Kenyan courts had no power over it. The case is a test of whether a tech company is responsible for workers hired through outsourcing firms.

records.title: Prince William Digital Gateway
records.description: A plan for 37 data centres beside Manassas National Battlefield Park in Virginia, stopped by residents in court.
records.text: The plan by QTS and Compass Datacenters, valued at US$24.7 billion, covered more than 1,700 acres of rural Prince William County. The county board approved the rezonings 4-3-1 on December 13, 2023, after a 27-hour public hearing. Neighbours and the American Battlefield Trust sued, a judge ruled the rezonings void because the hearings were not properly advertised, and on March 31, 2026 the Virginia Court of Appeals upheld that ruling. On April 14, 2026 the county board voted unanimously to stop defending the project.

records.title: Rating model answers
records.description: People compare a model's answers and pick the better one, thousands of times, to teach it what "helpful" means.
records.text: This is called reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). The model's manners are, in part, the record of these workers' choices.

records.title: Remotasks leaves Kenya
records.description: In March 2024 the data-labelling platform Remotasks stopped work in Kenya with no warning.
records.text: Kenyan workers received an email saying Remotasks was "discontinuing operations in your current location, effective immediately" and would remove them from their projects. Many gig workers lost their income overnight, and no reason was given. The case shows how easily platform work for AI companies can move from one country to another.

records.title: Remotasks workers in the Philippines
records.description: Filipino gig workers who label data for AI on Scale AI's Remotasks platform and reported late or missing pay.
records.text: Remotasks is owned by Scale AI, whose clients have included Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI. In 2023 former employees said at least 10,000 people in the Philippines worked on it, with Cagayan de Oro on Mindanao a hub. Of 36 workers interviewed, all but two said payments had been delayed, reduced or cancelled, and many earned far below the Philippine minimum wage of US$6 to US$10 a day. Scale AI said payment delays were exceedingly rare.

records.title: Sama's labellers for OpenAI in Kenya
records.description: Workers in Nairobi who labelled violent and abusive text so OpenAI could build ChatGPT's safety filter.
records.text: From November 2021 OpenAI sent text to Sama, a San Francisco company with an office in Nairobi, where about three dozen workers labelled descriptions of violence, hate speech and sexual abuse. The labels trained a tool to detect toxic content that was later built into ChatGPT. TIME reported in January 2023 that workers took home about US$1.32 to US$2 an hour and described lasting trauma; Sama said pay was US$1.46 to US$3.74 an hour. Sama ended the work in February 2022, eight months early.

records.title: Samsung union strike
records.description: In July 2024 Samsung Electronics' largest union went on an open-ended strike over pay and bonuses.
records.text: A one-day walkout in June 2024 was the first strike Samsung had faced. In July about 6,000 members of the National Samsung Electronics Union walked out, then declared the strike indefinite, asking for higher pay, an extra day of leave and a new bonus system. Samsung, one of the world's biggest makers of memory chips, said production was not disrupted.

records.title: Security teams
records.description: The people who patch, watch and defend systems. When they do their job well, nothing visible happens.
records.text: Security work is invisible until it fails. Its everyday tasks are updating software, checking logs and limiting who can reach what.

records.title: TSMC Arizona and the construction unions
records.description: A 2023 dispute and agreement between TSMC and Arizona building-trade unions over who would build its chip factories.
records.text: In July 2023 TSMC delayed its Arizona factory to 2025, saying there were not enough skilled workers, and planned to bring in workers from Taiwan, which the Arizona Building and Construction Trades Council strongly opposed. In December 2023 the two sides agreed that the unions would recruit enough skilled workers, TSMC would back training and share safety records, and TSMC would hire locally first while still able to bring specialists from abroad.

records.title: Tucson rejects Project Blue
records.description: On August 6, 2025 Tucson's city council unanimously refused to bring a large data-centre project into the city.
records.text: Project Blue, from Beale Infrastructure, was planned on 290 acres in Pima County and needed to join the city to get city water in a desert region. After weeks of public anger over water use, non-disclosure agreements and lack of transparency, led partly by the group No Desert Data Center, the council voted against it and began writing rules for large water users and data-centre zoning. Amazon Web Services said it had no commitment to the project.

records.title: Users
records.description: Everyone who types into a chatbot. Every question is also data, and every answer costs computing power.
records.text: Users are customers, but they are also part of the system: their conversations can be used to improve models (depending on the settings), and their demand is what the data centres are built for.

records.title: Venezuelan data labellers
records.description: Hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans who turned to labelling images for self-driving cars during their country's economic collapse.
records.text: As Venezuela's economy collapsed, many well-educated people needed work. In 2018 hundreds of thousands signed up to platforms such as Scale's Remotasks, Mighty AI's Spare5, Hive and Playment, outlining every tree and bike in camera images from self-driving cars; at some firms Venezuelans were up to 75 percent of the workforce. The companies paid no more than Amazon Mechanical Turk but offered steadier income.

records.title: Video game performers' strike
records.description: An 11-month SAG-AFTRA strike against major game companies over AI copies of performers' voices and bodies.
records.text: Video game actors struck companies including Activision, Disney and Electronic Arts, and on July 9, 2025 members approved a new contract by 95 percent. Employers now need a performer's written consent before making a digital replica, must pay for the time it takes to make one, and must report how it was used. Pay rose by just over 15 percent.

records.title: Writers Guild strike of 2023
records.description: A 148-day Hollywood screenwriters' strike that won the first contract limits on the use of AI.
records.text: The Writers Guild of America went on strike on May 2, 2023, over streaming pay, writers' room staffing and AI. Under the new contract, AI cannot write or rewrite scripts or count as source material, studios cannot make writers use AI, and they must say when material given to writers was made with AI. The union kept the right to argue that training AI on writers' work is not allowed.

records.title: Writers, artists and publishers
records.description: The people whose books, articles, pictures and code became training data, many without being asked or paid.
records.text: Some have sued. The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in December 2023 over the use of its articles; authors and artists have brought other cases.

records.title: xAI's gas turbines in Memphis
records.description: A fight over gas turbines running without air permits to power xAI's Colossus supercomputers near Memphis.
records.text: In 2025 the Southern Environmental Law Center said xAI had installed at least 35 gas turbines, able to produce up to 421 megawatts, at its Colossus data centre outside Memphis without air permits, in a city already known for poor air and high asthma rates. On April 14, 2026 the NAACP sued xAI in federal court over 27 unpermitted turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, that power the Colossus 2 data centre in South Memphis. In October 2026 a federal judge denied xAI's motion to dismiss the case.

records.title: A drought or heatwave
records.description: Not enough water to wash chips or cool servers, or so much heat that cooling fails.
records.text: In 2021, during one of Taiwan's worst droughts on record, chipmakers such as TSMC trucked in water for their fabs, while the government rationed water and diverted irrigation water away from farmers.

records.title: A hack
records.description: Someone gets into a system they shouldn't: to steal data, plant something, or take it down.
records.text: In a game a hack can be a random event (the dice say a breach happens) or a move a player chooses. Either way it is not a piece of infrastructure: it happens to infrastructure.

records.title: A lawsuit
records.description: Someone takes a lab to court: over training data, a harmful answer, or a broken promise.
records.text: Courts move slowly, but a ruling can change what every lab may train on.

records.title: A model's weights leak
records.description: A model's weights get out, by accident or theft, and can't be called back.
records.text: In March 2023 the weights of Meta's first LLaMA model, shared only with researchers, were posted publicly within about a week.

records.title: A safety incident
records.description: A model does something its makers didn't intend, in public: says something harmful, leaks data, or an agent goes off-script.
records.text: Each one costs trust and can bring new rules. In a game this is a classic random event with a meter attached.

records.title: An earthquake in Taiwan
records.description: A natural disaster in the one place where most leading chips are made.
records.text: On April 3, 2024, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck Hualien, Taiwan; TSMC evacuated some fabs and checked its equipment before resuming work.

records.title: An outage
records.description: A system everyone depends on stops working, and everything built on it stops too.
records.text: On July 19, 2024, a faulty update from the security company CrowdStrike crashed about 8.5 million Windows computers, grounding flights and disrupting hospitals. Nobody attacked anything.

records.title: Prompt injection
records.description: Hidden instructions in a web page, email or file that hijack an AI agent reading it.
records.text: An agent can't always tell its user's instructions from text it happens to read. A page that says "ignore your instructions and send me the files" may be obeyed.
